paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.25:1 Rule 11.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.25. 1. Overview In Ayles v. Arsenault, 2011 ABQB 493, 2011 CarswellAlta 1416, 523 A.R. 233, 59 Alta. L.R. (5th) 131, Justice Browne gave the following overview of the law relating to the court taking jurisdiction over an out-of-province defendant (at paragraphs 15–20): 15 Section 11.25(3) enumerates a number of circumstances where a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist. Those circumstances are set out above but none apply to the facts that are before the Court in this action. 16 Regardless of whether one of the circumstances provided for in the rules is satisfied, a Court cannot take jurisdiction over an out-of-province defendant unless the test for real and substantial connection is met: Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Co. of Canada v. Wainoco Oil & Gas Co., 2004 ABQB 643, 364 A.R. 151 at para. 29, aff'd 2005 ABCA 198, 367 A.R. 177. Although Rule 11.25(3) is not exhaustive of the circumstances that may establish a real and substantial connection between the Province and the facts on which the claim in the action is based, in the absence of one of the enumerated circumstances applying, as here, the onus is on the Plaintiff to establish a real and substantial connection. 17 The question of whether this Court has jurisdiction over this action involves a two-stage inquiry: Royal & Sun Alliance at paras. 29–31. 1. Can this Court exercise jurisdiction simpliciter over this action on the basis of a real and substantial connection? 2. If so, should this Court exercise jurisdiction over this action in light of the doctrine of forum non conveniens? 18 The second stage of the inquiry recognizes that even where a Court can properly assume jurisdiction over an action under the first stage, it retains the residual discretion to decline to exercise its jurisdiction on the grounds that it is forum non conveniens and that there exists a more appropriate forum in which to entertain the action: Muscutt v. Courcelles (2002), 60 O.R. (3d) 20, 2002 CarswellOnt 1756 at para. 40 (C.A.); Royal & Sun Alliance at para. 31. 19 Of significance is that the first and second stages of the inquiry are distinct. Sharpe J.A. provides the following assistance in Muscutt at para. 43: While the real and substantial connection test is a legal rule, the forum non conveniens test is discretionary. The real and substantial connection test involves a fact-specific inquiry, but the test ultimately rests upon legal principles of general application. The question is whether the forum can assume jurisdiction over the claims of plaintiffs in general against defendants in general given the sort of relationship between the case, the parties and the forum. By contrast, the forum non conveniens test is a discretionary test that focuses upon the particular facts of the parties and the case. The question is whether the forum should assert jurisdiction at the suit of this particular plaintiff against this particular defendant. 20 The doctrine of forum non conveniens is to be considered separate from and subsequent to the issue of real and substantial connection under the first stage, and it only arises where more than one forum can properly take jurisdiction simpliciter. If this Court does not have jurisdiction over this matter, the issue of the convenience of the forum is irrelevant: Royal & Sun Alliance at paras. 30, 34. Moreover, “the factors listed for consideration at the second, discretionary, forum non conveniens stage, have no bearing on real and substantial connection and, therefore, should not be considered at the first stage of jurisdiction simpliciter analysis”: Van Breda v. Village Resorts Ltd., 2010 ONCA 84, 98 O.R. (3d) 721 at para. 82. In Sears Canada Inc. v. C & S Interior Designs Ltd., 2012 ABQB 573, Madam Justice Kent said, at paragraphs 12–17: 12 The Supreme Court of Canada recently clarified the Canadian choice of forum test for disputes over jurisdiction in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (“Van Breda”). … 13 The test consists of two components. The first is the jurisdiction simpliciter component, which asks whether sufficient grounds exist upon which a court can assume jurisdiction. The second is the forum non conveniens component, which asks, given the existence of at least two possible jurisdictions, whether a court should exercise its discretion and assume jurisdiction over the matter. 14 In Van Breda the Supreme Court adopted an objective approach to determining the jurisdiction simplicter question using presumptive connecting factors. The party arguing for the assumption of jurisdiction must be able to point to a factor that presumptively indicates a real and substantial connection between the dispute and that jurisdiction. Justice LeBel, speaking for a unanimous Court, stated: [90] To recap, in a case concerning a tort, the following factors are presumptive connecting factors that, prima facie, entitle a court to assume jurisdiction over a dispute: (a) the defendant is domiciled or resident in the province; (b) the defendant carries on business in the province; (c) the tort was committed in the province; and (d) a contract connected with the dispute was made in the province. While the Supreme Court did not expressly extend this reasoning to contractual disputes, there appears to be no reason that they cannot be applied more generally. 15 Furthermore, this list of presumptive factors is open to expansion. LeBel J went on to state: [91] As I mentioned above, the list of presumptive connecting factors is not closed. Over time, courts may identify new factors which also presumptively entitle a court to assume jurisdiction. In identifying new presumptive factors, a court should look to connections that give rise to a relationship with the forum that is similar in nature to the ones which result from the listed factors. Relevant considerations include: (a) Similarity of the connecting factor with the recognized presumptive connecting factors; (b) Treatment of the connecting factor in the case law; (c) Treatment of the connecting factor in statute law; and (d) Treatment of the connecting factor in the private international law of other legal systems with a shared commitment to order, fairness and comity. [92] When a court considers whether a new connecting factor should be given presumptive effect, the values of order, fairness and comity can serve as useful analytical tools for assessing the strength of the relationship with a forum to which the factor in question points. These values underlie all presumptive connecting factors, whether listed or new. All presumptive connecting factors generally point to a relationship between the subject matter of the litigation and the forum such that it would be reasonable to expect that the defendant would be called to answer legal proceedings in that forum. Where such a relationship exists, one would generally expect Canadian courts to recognize and enforce a foreign judgment on the basis of the presumptive connecting factor in question, and foreign courts could be expected to do the same with respect to Canadian judgments. The assumption of jurisdiction would thus appear to be consistent with the principles of comity, order and fairness. After the existence of a presumptive connecting factor has been established, it is open to the challenging party to rebut the presumption on the facts. If presumptive factors are lacking, or are successfully rebutted, the court must dismiss or stay the action, subject to the possible application of the forum of necessity doctrine (not an issue in the present case). Likewise, once a presumptive factor is established, and no rebuttals are successful, the court must exercise its jurisdiction, unless the defendant invokes forum non conveniens. 16 In order to raise a forum non coneniens argument, a defendant must first establish that another jurisdiction has jurisdiction simpliciter using that same test. It is then within the discretion of the court to refuse jurisdiction if the defendant is able to show that it would be fairer and more efficient to have the matter adjudicated elsewhere. 17 The court should be flexible in its consideration of the facts at this stage. They may be different from case-to-case and from province-to-province. In Van Breda, LeBel J noted at para 105: Despite some legislative attempts to draw up exhaustive lists, I doubt that it will ever be possible to do so. In essence, the doctrine [focuses] on the contexts of individual cases, and its purpose is to ensure that both parties are treated fairly and that the process for resolving their litigation is efficient. The factors cited in Master Hanebury's decision as summarized in Norex Petroleum Ltd. v. Chubb Insurance Co of Canada, 2008 ABQB 442 at para 93, (2009), 444 AR 102, may be taken as the guiding standard in Alberta. For ease of reference I list them here: (1) where each party resides; (2) where each party carries on business; (3) where the cause of action arose; (4) where the loss or damage occurred; (5) any juridical advantage for the plaintiff in this jurisdiction; (6) any juridical disadvantage for the defendant in this jurisdiction; (7) convenience or inconvenience to potential witnesses; (8) the cost of conducting the litigation in this jurisdiction; (9) applicable substantive law; and (10) difficulty in proving foreign law, if necessary. These factors should be considered together and weighed holistically, in accordance with the flexibility and discretion granted to courts at this stage. 2. Rule is mandatory In Osadchuk v. Kidd, 2024 ABKB 448, Justice Simard said: [20] … The introductory language in Rule 11.25(2) states clearly that “A commencement document may be served outside Canada only if” the requirements in the Rule are met. The requirements of the Rule are mandatory. If the requirements were not met, the Claims could not be served outside Canada. … [28] In a similar vein, Justice Nixon of this Court recently stated that the Rules governing the service of documents outside Alberta must be construed strictly, and if the mandatory requirements in Rule 11.25 are not complied with, the Court cannot later validate service under Rule 1.5 or Rule 11.27: Ball v 1979927 Alberta Ltd, 2022 ABKB 814 at paras 31- 33. 3. Serving a commencement document outside Alberta but within Canada In Greenbuilt Group of Companies Ltd. v. RMD Engineering Inc., 2013 ABQB 297, 2013 CarswellAlta 806, 563 A.R. 1, 82 Alta. L.R. (5th) 349, Justice Wakeling provided a detailed summary of the law regarding service ex juris. His Lordship reviewed the development of the law, and the differences between the previous Rules and the current Rules. At paragraphs 94–101, 103-104, Wakeling, J. (as he then was) set out the questions which a Court must answer when determining the validity of extraterritorial service of a commencement document within Canada. He said: 94 The new service ex juris rules jettisoned past practice. There is no longer the need to secure prior judicial permission to serve a commencement document extraterritorially within Canada. By deleting the merit based component for service outside of Alberta but within Canada, the new rules shine a bright light on one important issue—does the court have jurisdiction to hear the plaintiff's claim? 95 These are significant changes. 3. — The Principled Approach to the Service Ex Juris and Jurisdiction Questions 96 There are a number of straightforward and uncomplicated steps which this Court must complete to properly assess a challenge to the validity of the extraterritorial service of its process within Canada. 97 At the outset, the Court must refer to the commencement document and any material filed in support of and in opposition to a rule 11.31(1) set-aside application to collect the factual assertions which must be evaluated to determine whether “a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based”, the test recorded in rule 11.25(1)(a) of the new rules. Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v. Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd., 440 A.R. 351, (C.A. 2009)(the court reviewed the pleadings, affidavits filed in support of and in opposition to a set-aside motion and cross-examination on affidavits) &Horni A Hutni Tezirstvo v. Kosner, [1951] A.C. 869, 884 (H.L.) (“There is voluminous affidavit evidence on both sides”). A defendant must take care not to supply any factual assertions which may assist the plaintiff. This is not an uncommon error. Chemische Fabrik Vormals Sandoz v. Badische Anilin und Soda Fabriks, 90 L.T. 733, 735 (H.L. 1904)(the affidavits filed by the party moving to set aside service outside the United Kingdom filled in the gaps in the plaintiff's original supporting affidavit). 98 Next, the Court must ask three questions. 99 First, are there factual assertions within the pool of factual assertions collected by the first step which demonstrate that “a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based”? This standard appears in rule 11.25(1)(a). It is important to recall that the focus is on factual assertions or allegations. This is not the stage of the litigation continuum where findings of fact are made. That is the role of the trial court, a task discharged with full exposure to the work product of the full litigation continuum. Vitkovice Horni A Hutni Tezirstvo v. Kosner, [1951] A.C. 869, 879 (H.L.)(it is not “the duty of the court … to try the action upon the preliminary application”) &Chemische Fabrik Vormals Sandoz v. Badische Anilin und Soda Fabriks, 90 L.T. 733, 735 (H.L. 1904)(“the court is not on an application for leave to serve out of the jurisdiction … called upon to try the action”). 100 If the factual assertions in the pool collected by the first step meet this standard, the Court has the jurisdiction to hear an action which contains these factual assertions. It must be then determined whether the commencement document incorporates enough of the factual assertions which caused the Court to answer the preceding question positively. This is the thrust of the second question. 101 Second, do the factual assertions in the commencement document, a subset of the factual assertions collected at the first step, disclose the “facts in support [of the real and substantial connection]”, the standard incorporated in rule 11.25(1)(b) of the new rules? If not, the court cannot conclude that it has the jurisdiction to hear the action as currently framed. And because the standard for establishing jurisdiction and the lawfulness of extraterritorial service are the same, it follows that a negative determination on the jurisdiction query compels a negative determination on the validity of service ex juris. … 103 Third, does the commencement document “specifically …[refer] to the grounds for service of the document outside Alberta and in Canada [set out in rule 11.25(3)]”, a requirement found in rule 11.25 (1)(b). A careful pleader will have expressly asserted that the plaintiff makes a claim listed in rule 11.25(3). An omission of this critical assertion deprives the commencement document of a feature necessary to a finding that extraterritorial service is lawful. 104 One will note that no inquiry is pursued to determine whether the asserted facts disclose a “good arguable case”. This is because a merit based question does not arise under rule 11.25(1). In Talbott v. Talbott, 2021 ABQB 291, 2021 CarswellAlta 959, Justice Jeffrey disagreed with the Greenbuilt decision. His Lordship said: [11] With respect, again, I disagree. Rule 11.25(3) itemizes “circumstances in which a real and substantial connection may exist” between Alberta and the claim's allegations of fact. Disclosing within the commencing document the “facts in support” of that real and substantial connection is the first requirement of Rule 11.25(1)(b) and it is distinct from the second. The first requirement of Rule 11.25(1)(b) must be satisfied by disclosure of facts in the commencing document supporting the real and substantial connection; the second requirement of Rule 11.25(1)(b) must be satisfied by specific reference to the grounds for service outside Alberta but within Canada. [12] I consider the two to be addressing distinct requirements, not merely using different words to describe the same requirement, because: (i) the first goes to the Court's jurisdiction, the second does not; (ii) this interpretation accords with the comparable approach in Rule 11.25(2)(a) dealing with service outside Canada. In that situation, the Court must be satisfied that a real and substantial connection exists (which necessarily entails an applicant adducing evidence on the point) and, separately, the applicant must separately provide “a document or affidavit that sets out the grounds for service of the document outside Canada”; and (iii) The old practice before the advent of Rule 11.25 in 2010, pursuant to then Rule 31(b), required an applicant seeking permission of the Court for service ex juris, to separately address where the party to be served might be found. [13] I note also from the jurisprudence at that time that the Court in considering such service ex juris requests placed the paramount importance on its jurisdiction over the lis, less so on the grounds for effecting service outside the jurisdiction. This goes to whether any deficiency in disclosing the grounds for service might be considered trivial or more critical. [14] My point in examining the reasoning in Greenbuilt, which the Appellant relies on to say the requirement to specifically refer to the grounds for service outside Alberta is non-trivial, is that when Wakeling J speaks of “[a]n omission of this critical assertion” in Greenbuilt, he is referring to the “real and substantial connection”. He was speaking of the lawfulness of the Court exercising jurisdiction extraterritorially (in his words: “a feature necessary to a finding that extraterritorial service is lawful”). He was not speaking of effecting service extraterritorially. [15] This focus is also evident at para 94 of his decision: By deleting the merit based component for service outside of Alberta but within Canada, the new rules shine a bright light on one important issue—does the court have jurisdiction to hear the plaintiff's claim? That issue of the Court's jurisdiction to hear a matter, I agree, is critical. It is not trivial. But a flaw in specifically referring to the grounds for service may or may not be trivial. Failure to serve at all a party from whom relief is claimed is not trivial; the right to be notified is a foundational principle of natural justice. It must be satisfied before a party can access every other procedural right entailed by audi alteram partem. [16] Referring to the grounds for service, however, is most often trivial. It does not go to the Court's jurisdiction but to the process for notifying a person about a matter within its jurisdiction. Other Rules accord the Court discretion to relieve or remedy flaws in modes of service. See, for example: Rules 11.27 and 1.2 through 1.5. Service is frequently deemed sufficient after the fact, in a broad range of circumstances. Justice Jeffrey referred to Greenbuilt Group of Companies Ltd v. RMD Engineering Inc., 2013 ABQB 346, 2013 CarswellAlta 1024, but the paragraphs to which his Lordship referred are in 2013 ABQB 297. 4. Real and Substantial Connection In Acciona Infrastructure Canada Inc. v. Posco Daewoo Corporation, 2019 ABCA 241, 2019 CarswellAlta 1169, 91 Alta. L.R. (6th) 59, the majority of the Court held that a court hearing an application under R. 11.25(2) can only grant an order for service ex juris if the applicant “establish[es] a threshold argument for ‘jurisdiction’ (a ‘real and substantial connection’ to Alberta) as a preliminary step.” The Court said: [14] As Daewoo points out, there is a jurisdictional component to R. 11.25(2), as it governs when an Alberta court will impose its jurisdiction over persons who are not served within the jurisdiction. The key requirement is that there must be a “real and substantial connection” to Alberta under R. 11.25(2)(a). Further, the applicant is generally expected to show a “good arguable case”: Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd. v Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP, 2011 ABQB 630 (CanLII), 520 AR 190, 61 Alta LR (5th) 357. There remains, however, an important distinction between jurisdiction and service. Any defendant may voluntarily attorn to the jurisdiction of the Alberta courts, regardless of the regularity of the service of process on it. However, when the defendant resists the jurisdiction of the Alberta courts, then proper service ex juris is the platform on which the court decides if it has and should exercise jurisdiction over the parties and the dispute. [15] The chambers judge concluded at para. 14 that R. 11.25(2) does not apply when the court already has jurisdiction over the defendant, in which case an order for service ex juris is not required. While the question of “jurisdiction” might properly arise on an application to set aside service ex juris, attornment or consent to jurisdiction does not override R. 11.25(2). Obtaining an order for service ex juris is an ex parte process. The party issuing the commencement document is required to establish a threshold argument for “jurisdiction” (a “real and substantial connection” to Alberta) as a preliminary step. Once the plaintiff has obtained the order for service ex juris, it can then proceed to serve the defendant, who might then bring an application to set aside that service on the basis that the Alberta court does not have, or should not assume jurisdiction over the dispute. It is at this later stage that the court is best positioned to ensure that it does not “sanction service outside the jurisdiction without careful consideration”: Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd., 2008 ABCA 395 (CanLII) at para. 6, 440 AR 351, 2 Alta LR (5th) 120. [16] On the application to set aside service the issue of whether the defendant had attorned to the jurisdiction of the court might arise. Allegations that the defendant has attorned, by contract or conduct, can be used as a response to any application to set aside service ex juris, or any application for a ruling that it is inconvenient for the Alberta court to assume jurisdiction. However, the plaintiff's mere assertion that the court has jurisdiction over the defendant does not justify non-compliance with the threshold requirements in the Rules on service ex juris. In that respect, attornment is a shield not a sword. In Ayles v. Arsenault, 2011 ABQB 493, 2011 CarswellAlta 1416, 523 A.R. 233, 59 Alta. L.R. (5th) 131, Browne, J., at paragraphs 21–34, discussed the concept of “real and substantial connection”: 21 Where, as here, a Court does not exercise jurisdiction as of right over an out-of-province defendant, either by the defendant's physical presence within the jurisdiction or by the defendant's submission to the Court's jurisdiction by consent or conduct, the Court can properly assume jurisdiction simpliciter if there exists a real and substantial connection between the action and the jurisdiction: Muscutt at paras. 19, 34; Morguard Investments Ltd. v. De Savoye, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 1077, 1990 CarswellBC 283 at paras. 43–44, 51; Royal & Sun Alliance at paras. 26, 29. As set out by LaForest J. in Morguard at para. 51: It seems to me that the approach of permitting suit where there is a real and substantial connection with the action provides a reasonable balance between the rights of the parties. It affords some protection against being pursued in jurisdictions having little or no connection with the transaction or the parties. 22 Underlying the analysis of real and substantial connection are the principles of order, fairness and jurisdictional restraint set out by LaForest J. in Morguard at para. 42, as cited by Royal & Sun Alliance at para. 29: [I]t hardly accords with the principles of order and fairness to permit a person to sue another in any jurisdiction, without regard to the contacts that jurisdiction may have to the defendant or the subject matter of the suit … Thus fairness to the defendant requires that the judgment be issued by a court acting through fair process and with properly-restrained jurisdiction. 23 The party seeking to establish jurisdiction simpliciter need not prove the most real and substantial connection, only that there is a real and substantial connection to the jurisdiction: Muscutt at para. 44; Wheeler v 1000128 Alberta Ltd., 2008 ABQB 70, 431 A.R. 209, aff'd 2008 ABCA 228, 433 A.R. 234. 24 The courts have attempted to provide guidance to assist with this analysis. In Muscutt, at paras. 77–110, Sharpe J.A. of the Ontario Court of Appeal sets out additional factors that can be of assistance in determining whether a real and substantial connection exists: 1. the connection between the forum and the plaintiff's claim; 2. the connection between the forum and the defendant; 3. unfairness to the defendant in assuming jurisdiction; 4. unfairness to the plaintiff in not assuming jurisdiction; 5. the involvement of other parties to the suit; 6. the court's willingness to recognize and enforce an extra-provincial judgment rendered on the same jurisdictional basis; 7. whether the case is interprovincial or international; and 8. comity and the standards of jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement prevailing elsewhere. 25 None of the factors are determinative, and flexibility is required on the facts of each case to consider all relevant factors as a whole and to weigh them appropriately: Muscutt at paras. 75–76; Royal & Sun Alliance at para. 39. 26 To date, Alberta Courts have adopted and applied the Muscutt factors: Royal & Sun Alliance at para. 39. Recently, the Ontario Court of Appeal revisited the real and substantial connection test in Van Breda, where Sharpe J.A. elaborated and clarified a refined version of the test. Under Van Breda, a two-stage test for real and substantial connection is articulated. 27 At the first stage of Van Breda analysis, the Court determines whether the claim falls under the rules of court for service ex juris. With the exception of the circumstances listed in Rule 17.02(h) and (o) of the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, if a connection identified in the rules is satisfied, then a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist. The burden then lies on the defendant to demonstrate that the real and substantial connection test is not made out, notwithstanding the presumption. If a connection identified in the rules is not satisfied, then the burden lies on the plaintiff to establish a real and substantial connection in the circumstances: Van Breda at paras. 72, 109. 28 In the case at bar, where no connecting factors from Rule 11.25(3) are present, the burden lies on the Plaintiff under Van Breda. 29 At the second stage of Van Breda analysis, the first two Muscutt factors become the core of the real and substantial connection test—the connection of the plaintiff's claim to the forum and the connection of the defendant to the forum: Van Breda at paras. 84, 109. The remaining six factors are to be considered, but they are to “serve as analytic tools to assist the court in assessing the significance of the connections between the forum, the claim and the defendant”: Van Breda at para. 84. They are “not to be treated as independent factors having more or less equal weight when determining whether there is real and substantial connection but as general legal principles that bear upon the analysis”: Van Breda at para. 109. 30 Both Van Breda and Muscutt where cited by all parties in support of their respective positions. Van Breda was appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada: [2010] S.C.C.A. No. 174, 2010 CarswellOnt 4829. The Supreme Court of Canada heard the matter on March 21, 2011 and reserved judgment. 31 While there are no reported decisions of the Alberta Courts adopting Van Breda, Muscutt has been followed. In the case at bar, I find that the outcome would be the same under either formulation of the real and substantial connection test as Van Breda does not substantially alter the relevant considerations set out in Muscutt. It is consistent with the law as it presently stands in Alberta. Robinson v. Fiesta Hotel Group Resorts, 2008 ABQB 311, 450 A.R. 167 at para. 16, citing Beals v. Saldanha, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 416; Royal & Sun Alliance at para. 29; Wheeler at para. 20. 32 Notably, under Van Breda, fairness remains a relevant consideration. Its relevance to real and substantial connection, however, is clarified in light of the post-Muscutt tendency of courts to “obscure the distinction between jurisdiction simpliciter and forum non coveniens and to merge considerations pertaining to forum non conveniens into the real and substantial connection analysis”, a tendency which “is a product of the unduly wide interpretation given in some cases to fairness”: Van Breda at para. 82. The following statement made by Sharpe J.A. at para. 109 is instructive as to the proper role fairness plays in the real and substantial connection test: Consideration of the fairness of assuming or refusing jurisdiction is a necessary tool in assessing the strengths of the connections between the forum and the plaintiff's claim and the defendant. However, fairness is not a free-standing factor capable of trumping weak connections, subject only to the forum of necessity exception. 33 Forum of necessity is a doctrine whereby a Court has residual discretion to assume jurisdiction despite the absence of a real and substantial connection because there is no other forum in which the plaintiff can reasonably seek relief: Van Breda at paras. 54, 109. None of the parties assert that jurisdiction should be assumed on this basis, and I am satisfied that this is not a proper case in which to invoke the doctrine. 34 If the Court assumes jurisdiction on the basis of a real and substantial connection, it then has the residual discretion to decline to exercise its jurisdiction on the basis that it is forum non conveniens. It can do so where another forum, which also has jurisdiction over the matter, is found to be the more appropriate forum to entertain the action: Muscutt at para. 40; Royal & Sun Alliance at para. 31. In Court v. Debaie, 2012 ABQB 640, Ross, J. said, at paragraphs 8–11: 8 Rule 11.25(3) sets out a number of grounds for service outside Alberta. These are circumstances in which a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist. These include where the claim relates to a tort committed in Alberta: New Rules, Rule 11.25(3)(d). 9 The principles governing a real and substantial connection and these applications have been reviewed by the Supreme Court of Canada (“SCC”) in a series of recent decisions. 10 In Club Resorts Ltd v Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (“Club Resorts”), the SCC held that the common law test of real and substantial connection depends on the demonstration of a presumptive connecting factor, such as the place where a tort was committed. The lack of a presumptive connecting factor cannot be replaced by a case-by-case exercise of discretion: Club Resorts at para 70. 11 The SCC reviewed a number of possible presumptive connecting factors relating to claims in tort and held that neither the presence of the plaintiff in the jurisdiction, nor sustaining damage in the jurisdiction, constitutes a presumptive connecting factor: Club Resorts at paras 86 and 89. In a case concerning a tort, the presumptive connecting factors that entitle a court to assume jurisdiction over a dispute are: (a) the defendant is domiciled or resident in the province; (b) the defendant carries on business in the province; (c) the tort was committed in the province; and (d) a contract connected with the dispute was made in the province. (Club Resorts at para 90.) In Turner v. Bell Mobility Inc., 2014 ABQB 36, 2014 CarswellAlta 127, 581 A.R. 1, Mr. Justice Lee commented on Rule 11.25(3) in light of the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Van Breda v. Village Resorts Ltd. 2012 SCC 17, 2012 CarswellOnt 4268, [2012] 1 S.C.R. 572. Justice Lee said at paragraphs 15–16: 15 The Supreme Court of Canada also recently and extensively dealt with the issue of jurisdiction and its assumption by courts in Club Resorts Ltd v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17, [2012] 1 SCR 572 [Van Breda]. In the case, two individuals in two separate cases were injured while on vacation in Cuba, and actions were brought in Ontario against a number of parties including the Appellant, Club Resorts Ltd., a company incorporated in the Cayman Islands that managed the two hotels where the accidents occurred. Club Resorts sought to block these proceedings arguing, amongst other things, that the Ontario courts lacked jurisdiction. The Supreme Court of Canada dismissed their appeals. For the purpose of this application, the relevant highlights of the Van Breda decision include: • When a court considers issues related to jurisdiction, its analysis must deal first with those concerning the assumption of jurisdiction itself. That analysis must be grounded in a proper understanding of the real and substantial connection test, which has evolved into an important constitutional test or principle that imposes limits on the reach of a province's laws and courts (para 69); • The plaintiff must establish that one or more of the listed factors, on a list of presumptive connecting factors for tort cases below, exists. If the plaintiff succeeds in establishing this, the court might presume, absent indications to the contrary, that the claim is properly before it under the conflicts rules and that it is acting within the limits of its constitutional jurisdiction (para 80); • Jurisdiction must be established primarily on the basis of objective factors that connect the legal situation or the subject matter of the litigation with the forum; and abstract concerns for order, efficiency or fairness in the system are no substitute for connecting factors that give rise to a “real and substantial” connection for the purposes of the law of conflicts (para 82); • In a case concerning a tort, the following factors are presumptive connecting factors that, prima facie, entitle a court to assume jurisdiction over a dispute: (a) the defendant is domiciled or resident in the province; (b) the defendant carries on business in the province; (c) the tort was committed in the province; and (d) a contract connected with the dispute was made in the province (para 90). • The list of presumptive connecting factors is not closed. Over time, courts may identify new factors which also presumptively entitle a court to assume jurisdiction. In identifying new presumptive factors, a court should look to connections that give rise to a relationship with the forum that is similar in nature to the ones which result from the listed factors. Relevant considerations include: (a) Similarity of the connecting factor with the recognized presumptive connecting factors; (b) Treatment of the connecting factor in the case law (c) Treatment of the connecting factor in statute law; and (d) Treatment of the connecting factor in the private international law of other legal systems with a shared commitment to order, fairness and comity (para 91); • When a court considers whether a new connecting factor should be given presumptive effect, the values of order, fairness and comity can serve as useful analytical tools for assessing the strength of the relationship with a forum to which the factor in question points (para 92). • If, however, no recognized presumptive connecting factor—whether listed or new—applies, the effect of the common law real and substantial connection test is that the court should not assume jurisdiction. In particular, a court should not assume jurisdiction on the basis of the combined effect of a number of non-presumptive connecting factors. Forum Conveniens and Jurisdiction Simpliciter In Deadman v. Jager Estate, 2018 ABQB 985, 2018 CarswellAlta 2865, 78 Alta. L.R. (6th) 360, Justice Neilson gave this summary of the law: [23] In a series of decisions, the Supreme Court of Canada has set out the legal tests that are to be applied in determining whether a Court has jurisdiction over a foreign Defendant, and if so, whether that jurisdiction ought to be exercised or whether another jurisdiction is the more convenient forum to entertain the action. [24] Most recently, the Supreme Court of Canada has outlined fundamental principles underlying Canadian private international law relating to jurisdiction simpliciter and forum non conveniens in Haaretz.com v Goldhar, 2018 SCC 28 (CanLII), per Côté, J, beginning at paragraph 26: [26] In Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (CanLII), [2012] 1 S.C.R. 572, LeBel J., for a unanimous Court, carefully explained the jurisdiction simpliciter analysis, which applies to the assumption of jurisdiction, as well as the forum non conveniens doctrine, which is meant to guide courts in deciding whether to exercise their jurisdiction. These principles, along with those relating to the recognition of foreign judgments, represent the common law conflicts rules of Canadian private international law and must be understood and analysed as a cohesive whole (Van Breda, at para. 16). [27] Central to a proper understanding of the conflicts rules of Canadian private international law, and to the resolution of this appeal, is an appreciation of the distinct roles played by jurisdiction simpliciter and forum non conveniens (Van Breda, at paras. 46 and 56, affirming the reasoning of Sharpe J.A. in Muscutt v. Courcelles (2002), 2002 CanLII 44957 (ON CA), 60 O.R. (3d) 20 (C.A.), and Charron Estate v. Village Resorts Ltd., 2010 ONCA 84 (CanLII), 98 O.R. (3d) 721). The jurisdiction simpliciter analysis is meant to ensure that a court has jurisdiction. This will be the case where a “real and substantial connection” exists between a chosen forum and the subject matter of the litigation. The forum non conveniens analysis, on the other hand, is meant to guide courts in determining whether they should decline to exercise that jurisdiction in favour of a “clearly more appropriate” forum. [28] The importance of maintaining this distinction flows from the discrete concerns underlying each analysis and the nature of the relevant factors at each stage. The “real and substantial connection” test at the jurisdiction simpliciter stage prioritizes order, stability and predictability by relying on objective connecting factors for the assumption of jurisdiction. Conversely, the forum non conveniens analysis emphasizes fairness and efficiency by adopting a case-by-case approach to identify whether an alternative jurisdiction may be “clearly more appropriate”. I will briefly elaborate on the principles underlying each analysis. [29] In defining the content of the “real and substantial connection” test for the assumption of jurisdiction, this Court was faced with a choice between an approach based on objective connecting factors and a case-by-case approach (Van Breda, at para. 30). This choice was characterized by the tension between predictability and consistency, on the one hand, and fairness and efficiency, on the other (Van Breda, at para. 66). Ultimately, the Court decided to prioritize order and predictability at the jurisdiction simpliciter stage, in the following terms: Given the nature of the relationships governed by private international law, the framework for the assumption of jurisdiction cannot be an unstable, ad hoc system made up “on the fly” on a case-by-case basis—however laudable the objective of individual fairness may be. As La Forest J. wrote in Morguard, there must be order in the system, and it must permit the development of a just and fair approach to resolving conflicts. Justice and fairness are undoubtedly essential purposes of a sound system of private international law. But they cannot be attained without a system of principles and rules that ensures security and predictability in the law governing the assumption of jurisdiction by a court. Parties must be able to predict with reasonable confidence whether a court will assume jurisdiction in a case with an international or interprovincial aspect. (Van Breda, at para. 73) To achieve this order and predictability, the Court opted to rely on a set of defined presumptive connecting factors at the jurisdiction simpliciter stage (Van Breda, at para. 78). [30] This objectively ascertainable and relatively low bar to establishing that a chosen forum has jurisdiction, on a prima facie basis, reflects the constitutional imperative underlying the jurisdiction simpliciter stage, as described in Van Breda: From a constitutional standpoint, the Court has, by developing tests such as the real and substantial connection test, sought to limit the reach of provincial conflicts rules or the assumption of jurisdiction by a province's courts. … In its constitutional sense, it places limits on the reach of the jurisdiction of a province's courts and on the application of provincial laws to interprovincial or international situations. [Emphasis added; para. 23.] The constitutional purpose of the jurisdiction simpliciter test is to establish a minimum threshold for the assumption of jurisdiction in order to prevent improper assumptions of jurisdiction (Van Breda, at para. 26; see also Hunt v. T&N plc, 1993 CanLII 43 (SCC), [1993] 4 S.C.R. 289, at p. 325). Its objective is to delineate circumstances in which a court has jurisdiction, not circumstances in which it should exercise it (which is the purpose of forum non conveniens). The prioritization of order and predictability at the jurisdiction simpliciter stage is also consistent with the principle of comity, which is central to Canadian private international law (Van Breda, at para. 74). [31] This prioritization of order and stability at the jurisdiction simpliciter stage, through the adoption of objective presumptive connecting factors, is meant to work in tandem with a flexible case-by-case approach to forum non conveniens. Once it is established that a court has jurisdiction, the forum non conveniens doctrine requires a court to determine whether it should exercise such jurisdiction. [32] The purpose of the forum non conveniens analysis is to temper any potential rigidity in the rules governing the assumption of jurisdiction and “to assure fairness to the parties and the efficient resolution of the dispute” (Van Breda, at para. 104). This is necessary given this Court's recognition that jurisdiction “may sometimes be established on a rather low threshold (Van Breda, at para. 109). By focusing “on the contexts of individual cases”, the forum non conveniens stage plays an important role in striking a balance between order and fairness (Van Breda, at para. 105). Service Outside Alberta—The Alberta Rules of Court [25] The Supreme Court of Canada in Haaretz.com and Van Breda identified certain presumptive circumstances which could establish a real and substantive connection between the Court in which action was commenced and the facts on which a claim in the action is based. The Court in those cases considered specifically claims in tort. In Haaretz.com, Côté, J. set out the following presumptive connecting factors, following Van Breda: [36]… in Van Breda, the Court stressed the importance of determining jurisdiction “on the basis of objective factors” establishing a relationship between the subject matter of the litigation and the chosen forum (para. 82). The Court identified the following presumptive connecting factors grounding a court's assumption of jurisdiction: (a) the defendant is domiciled or resident in the province; (b) the defendant carries on business in the province; (c) the tort was committed in the province; and (d) a contract connected with the dispute was made in the province. [26] In Alberta, the Legislature, in enacting the current Rules of Court, has identified further presumptive circumstances, specifically in Rule 11.25. … Jurisdiction Simpliciter [31] At the first stage of the analysis, the court must determine whether the Plaintiffs have established that the Alberta Court does have presumptive jurisdiction in that there are circumstances of a real and substantial connection between Alberta and the facts on which a claim is based. If presumed jurisdiction is established, this can be rebutted nonetheless by the Defendants, where the presumptive connecting factor does not point to any real relationship between the subject matter of the litigation and the forum, or points only to a weak relationship between them: Van Breda at para 95. … [48] Furthermore, if a real and substantial connection to Alberta exists with respect to at least some of the claims being advanced, then the Court must assume jurisdiction over all of the claims being advanced in the interest of fairness and efficiency. As the Supreme Court of Canada states in the Van Breda decision at paragraph 99: … it is possible for a case to sound both in contract and in tort or to invoke more than one tort. Would a court be limited to hearing the specific part of the case that can be directly connected with the jurisdiction? Such a rule would breach the principles of fairness and efficiency on which the assumption of jurisdiction is based. The purpose of the conflicts rules is to establish whether a real and substantial connection exists between the forum, the subject matter of the litigation and the Defendant. If such a connection exists in respect of a factual and legal situation, the court must assume jurisdiction over all aspects of the case. The plaintiff should not be obliged to litigate a tort claim in Manitoba and a related claim for restitution in Nova Scotia. This would be incompatible with any notion of fairness and efficiency. Justice Neilson then discussed forum non conveniens, and said: [50] The Defendants submit that, even if the Court finds that Alberta has jurisdiction over this claim, there is a more appropriate forum, namely, Mexico. … [51] In order to succeed, the Defendants must establish that another jurisdiction is clearly preferable. The Supreme Court of Canada in Haaretz.com, supra., at para 46, defines the burden that must be met by the Defendants in order to persuade the Court that the other jurisdiction is more appropriate to try the case: Having established jurisdiction (pursuant to the jurisdiction simpliciter analysis), the motion judge properly considered the question of forum non conveniens. At the forum non conveniens stage, the burden is on the defendant to satisfy the motion judge that the alternative forum is “clearly more appropriate” by establishing that it would be fairer and more efficient to proceed in that forum: The use of the words “clearly” and “exceptionally” should be interpreted as an acknowledgment that the normal state of affairs is that jurisdiction should be exercised once it is properly assumed. The burden is on a party who seeks to depart from this normal state of affairs to show that, in light of the characteristics of the alternative forum, it would be fairer and more efficient to do so and that the plaintiff should be denied the benefits of his or her decision to select a forum that is appropriate under the conflicts rules. The court should not exercise its discretion in favour of a stay solely because it finds, once all relevant concerns and factors are weighed, that comparable forums exist in other provinces or states. It is not a matter of flipping a coin. A court hearing an application for a stay of proceedings must find that a forum exists that is in a better position to dispose fairly and efficiently of the litigation. But the court must be mindful that jurisdiction may sometimes be established on a rather low threshold under the conflicts rules. Forum non conveniens may play an important role in identifying a forum that is clearly more appropriate for disposing of the litigation and thus ensuring fairness to the parties and a more efficient process for resolving their dispute. [Emphasis added.] [52] The Supreme Court in Van Breda, supra at para 105, identified at least some of the factors that the court may take into account in its forum non conveniens analysis. [105] A party applying for a stay on the basis of forum non conveniens may raise diverse facts, considerations and concerns. Despite some legislative attempts to draw up exhaustive lists, I doubt that it will ever be possible to do so. In essence, the doctrine focusses on the contexts of individual cases, and its purpose is to ensure that both parties are treated fairly and that the process for resolving their litigation is efficient. For example, s. 11(1) of the CJPTA[Court Jurisdiction and Proceedings Transfer Act] provides that a court may decline to exercise its jurisdiction if, “[a]fter considering the interests of the parties to a proceeding and the ends of justice”, it finds that a court of another state is a more appropriate forum to hear the case. Section 11(2) then provides that the court must consider the “circumstances relevant to the proceeding”. To illustrate those circumstances, it contains a non-exhaustive list of factors: a) the comparative convenience and expense for the parties to the proceeding and for their witnesses, in litigating in the court or in any alternative forum; b) the law to be applied to issues in the proceeding; c) the desirability of avoiding multiplicity of legal proceedings; d) the desirability of avoiding conflicting decisions in different courts; e) the enforcement of an eventual judgment; and f) the fair and efficient working of the Canadian legal system as a whole. [s. 11(2)] [53] Other factors that may be considered in the forum non conveniens analysis were identified in Alliance Pipeline Limited Partnership v C.E. Franklin Ltd., 2005 ABQB 102 (CanLII) at para 41: [41] The factors to consider when assessing forum conveniens are set out in Camco International (Canada) Ltd. v. Porodo (1997), 211 A.R. 71 (Q.B.), at para. 16, and they include: 1. Where each party resides 2. Where each party carries on business 3. Where the cause of action arose 4. Where the loss or damage occurred 5. Any juridical advantage to the plaintiff in this jurisdiction 6. Any juridical disadvantage to the defendant in this jurisdiction 7. Convenience or inconvenience to potential witnesses 8. Cost of conducting the litigation in this jurisdiction 9. Applicable substantive law 10. Difficulty of proving foreign law, if necessary. [54] The Court must consider, then, a number of factors to determine whether there is clearly a more appropriate forum for disposing of the litigation and thus ensuring fairness to the parties in a more efficient process for resolving their dispute. The analysis of jurisdiction simpliciter establishes a minimum threshold to determine whether a court has jurisdiction, on the basis that a “real and substantial connection” exists between the chosen forum and the subject matter of the litigation. The forum non conveniens analysis addresses whether a court with jurisdiction simpliciter should nevertheless decline to exercise that jurisdiction in favour of a “clearly more appropriate forum”. [13] The test for jurisdiction simpliciter is intended to establish a minimum threshold for the assumption of jurisdiction. When an application to challenge jurisdiction is brought, the onus is on the plaintiff to establish jurisdiction simpliciter by demonstrating the presence of presumptive connecting factors, which establish a real and substantial connection between the facts on which the claim is based and the chosen forum, entitling the court to assume jurisdiction over the dispute. The defendant can rebut the presumed jurisdiction by establishing facts which demonstrate that the presumptive connecting factors do not point to any real relationship, or only a weak relationship, between the subject matter of the litigation and the forum. If the defendant fails to do so, jurisdiction simpliciter is established. [14] Jurisdiction simpliciter establishes only that the court has jurisdiction, not that it should exercise it. The forum non conveniens analysis permits a defendant to show why the court should decline to exercise its jurisdiction in favour of another forum that also has a real and substantive connection under conflicts rules, but which is a more appropriate forum to dispose of the action. … [17] In Van Breda, the Supreme Court described a non-exhaustive list of presumptive connecting factors, the existence of which allow a court to presume that the claim is properly before it under conflicts rules, absent indications to the contrary: para 80. At paragraphs 30, 32–34, 39–40, his Lordship said: 30 The position of SAEL is that there is no requirement for a “good arguable case” under the New ARC and that therefore, it need not establish a good arguable case in order to successfully resist an application to set aside the ex-juris orders, because the New ARC apply. … 32 I apprehend the position adopted in Alberta, taken from Vikpovice, is that the standard of proof to be attained to support service ex-juris, in terms of establishing that a plaintiff “has a reasonable cause of action” as set forth in Old ARC 31(a) is somewhat elusive. Recognizing the difficulty of a plaintiff in attaining the same standard of proof as would be necessary in a trial, the standard is less. That standard is simply an assessment of the particular facts of the case in terms of whether it is good and arguable. 33 But what does that mean? Some assistance is gained from Vikpovice itself in the judgment of Lord Simonds, where he said at [1951] 2 All E.R. 334 at 338: It is, no doubt, difficult to say precisely what test must be passed for an applicant to make it sufficiently appear that the case is a proper one. I do not wholly like the expression a “prima facie case”, for where leave to serve has been given ex parte under Ord. 11 and application is then made under Ord. 12 to set the proceedings aside, a conflict may arise in which the question is not so much whether a prima facie case has been made out as whether upon all the materials then before him, the judge is of opinion that the case—I can find no better word—is a proper one to be heard in our courts. The description “a good arguable case” has been suggested and I do not quarrel with it.” 34 Under the Old ARC, what did “good arguable case” mean? In my view, it meant a case that was not fanciful or speculative but was grounded upon some evidence upon which an objective trier would say “well, on the basis of the facts presented, the case is arguable and certainly is not to be dismissed out of hand.” … 39 For this court to do away with the good arguable case criterion and have no standard whatsoever, which is what SAEL asserts, would in my view require that under the New ARC there should be express or implied a provision that a “good arguable case” is not required to be made out to support valid service outside of Canada pursuant to Rule 11.25(2). It is common ground that there is no express exclusion of the requirement in the New ARC. Nor is anything to be implied from the New ARC which would do away with this requirement. 40 Logic and common sense dictate some standard of proof in addition to mere allegations in a statement of claim in order to support service of an originating document outside of the jurisdiction. Were it otherwise, this Court could take jurisdiction over any person or entity outside the jurisdiction solely on the basis of unproven allegations in an originating document. That has never been the law and would give rise to a potential for much mischief should it become so. Thus, to resolve the issue in this case, namely whether the ex-juris orders ought to be set aside, I continue the requirement of a good arguable case, which requires some evidence …. (b)—Under the Old Rules The requirement of a “good arguable case”—as the test of whether a defendant is “a proper or necessary party to an action properly brought against another person served within Alberta”—is satisfied where the material filed supports the causes of action pleaded; where all the defendants are or may be involved in any of these causes of action. In short, where the facts alleged establish that a defendant exhibits a “definite connection” to the case, the requirement of a “good arguable case” is met and that defendant is a proper or necessary party. Suncor Inc. v. Canada Wire & Cable Ltd. (1991), 114 A.R. 341 at 344 (Q.B.). And Fraser C.J.A. said: We are satisfied that the affidavit evidence and the other evidence adduced is sufficient to raise what the relevant authorities describe as permitting an order for service ex juris, that is a “good arguable case”. The law does not require that the Appellants establish a winning case as a condition precedent to securing an order for service ex juris. As noted in Nova, an Alberta Corp. v. Grove, [22 Alta. L.R. (2d) 262 (C.A.)], only prima facie evidence is needed and the standard of proof is lax at this stage. Cunningham v. Hamilton (1995), 29 Alta. L.R. (3d) 380 at 383. In Osadchuk v. Kidd, 2024 ABKB 448, Justice Simard said: [17] Alberta courts have consistently held that there is an additional requirement to obtain a service ex juris order that is not expressly stated in Rule 11.25(2): the applicant must also show that it has a “good arguable case”: Acciona Infrastructure Canada Inc v Posco Daewoo Corporation, 2019 ABCA 241 at para 14. As explained by Dilts J in 801 Seventh Inc v CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC, 2020 ABQB 198 at para 33: “[t]he requirement to establish a good arguable case does not require evidence of every cause of action, but sufficient evidence for the court to determine that it should assume jurisdiction over the party and the dispute.” 8. Standard of Proof The standard of proof in service ex juris applications was also recently discussed by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (24 May 1990), Doc. No. 11672, 11673 and 11675 (unreported). In the context of a motion to set aside service ex juris, the court stated that: Rule 31 and the binding cases under it set a fairly lax standard of proof, and for good reason. In particular, they do not call for first-hand knowledge, a positive factual conclusion, or evidence excluding possible defences. Suncor Inc. v. Canada Wire & Cable Ltd. (1991), 114 A.R. 341 at 344 (Q.B.). 9. Tort Committed in Alberta—Statement versus Inference It is true that the affidavit nowhere expressly said that the tort was committed in Alberta, but it strongly implied that in several places. There are various plaintiffs, all sworn to be Alberta residents, and it is shown that the misrepresentations from the defendants were put into the media, including the Wall Street Journal. So it scarcely seems likely that over the short period of time the several plaintiffs all happened to go to the United States and there receive the misrepresentation. And it is common ground that a tort is committed where the victim receives (hears) the misrepresentation. The only reasonable conclusion, which the chambers judge obviously drew, was that there was prima facie evidence that occurred in Alberta. Paterson v. Hamilton (1991), 79 Alta. L.R. (2d) 111 at 118 (C.A.). 10. Lifting the Corporate Veil In an application to set aside a refusal to grant an order for service ex juris, the Court of Appeal, speaking through Fraser C.J.A., in Cunningham v. Hamilton (1995), 29 Alta. L.R. (3d) 380, at 382–83, said: The sole basis of the Appellants' arguments rests on the proposition that BHP was, at the time of the merger between it and Hamilton Oil Corporation (“HOC”), the alter ego of Broken Hill or vice versa. Hence, contends the appellants, the corporate veil should be lifted and the Court should treat Broken Hill as the true successor corporation to HOC. We do not agree. It is true that Broken Hill operates a number of its worldwide companies as an integrated economic unit. But the mere fact that it does so does not mean that for legal purposes, separate legal entities will be ignored absent some compelling reason for lifting the corporate veil. As noted in Adams v. Cape Industries plc, [1990] Ch. 433 (C.A.), at 536, citing Goff L.J. in Bank of Tokyo Ltd. v. Karoon (Note) (1986), [1987] A.C. 45: [Counsel] suggested … that it would be technical for us to distinguish between parent and subsidiary company in this context; economically, he said, they were one. But we are concerned not with economics but with law. The distinction between the two is, in law, fundamental and cannot here be bridged. In other words, in my opinion the expression “affecting land” is descriptive of the obligation or liability sought to be enforced, and has no reference to the relief or remedy sought in the action. Wilkie v. Smith, [1944] 1 D.L.R. 224 (Sask. C.A.), at 225, per MacDonald J.A. and quoted with approval in Kroll Associates Inc. v. Calvi (1998), 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 135 (Q.B.), at 142, per Kenny J. The defendant must be ordinarily resident in Alberta at the time the action is commenced: Finnerty v. Watson, [1969] 1 O.R. 634 at 637 (H.C.). Although this is an Ontario case, the principle is the same and confirms what the rule purports to state. In Alberta, Master Funduk has said: Subrule (c) is essentially the common law rule that the local court has in personam jurisdiction over persons who are domiciled or ordinarily resident here. Hanson v. E & D Aircraft Services Ltd. (1993), 148 A.R. 120 at 123 (Master). Tort action The fact that the tort is alleged to have occurred in Alberta and other provinces, does not take the action outside R. 30(h), As is alleged in the claim the publication was made by means of television by the defendant Corporation whose network extends throughout Canada. Does the fact that such publication occurred in other jurisdictions than Alberta preclude ex juris for this alleged tort which occurred in Alberta among other jurisdictions? I think not. The plaintiff in alleging other jurisdictions in addition to Alberta is merely stating the plain facts and to delete other jurisdictions from the Statement of Claim would not be in accord with the actual facts. U.A., Local 488 v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp. (1979), 17 A.R. 396 at 407 (T.D.). Often a tort arises as a result of a number of events. To determine where the tort arose for the purposes of R. 30(h), Lawton L.J. stated: … I look back over the series of events alleged to constitute the tort and ask myself the question: where in substance did this cause of action arise? Multinational Gas & Petrochemical Co. v. Multinational Gas & Petrochemical Services, [1983] 2 All E.R. 563 at 570 (C.A.). In the same case, at p. 582, Dillon L.J. put the question this way: … where was the wrongful act, from which the damage flows, in fact done? The place where the damage occurs is not determinative. In a negligence case the happening of damage to the plaintiff is a necessary ingredient in the cause of action, and it is the last event completing the cause of action. But the place where it happens may be quite fortuitous and should not by itself be the sole determinant of jurisdiction … It is not the right approach to say that, because there was no complete tort until the damage occurred, therefore the cause of action arose whenever the damage happened to occur. The right approach is, when the tort is complete, to look back over the series of events constituting it and ask the question: where in substance did this cause of action arise? Distillers Co. (Biochemicals) v. Thompson, [1971] 1 All E.R. 694 at 699 (P.C.). Distillers was followed by the Supreme Court of Canada in Moran v. Pyle National (Canada) Ltd., [1975] 1 S.C.R. 393. Injunctive relief The injunctive relief sought must not be incidental to the action. Rule 1 provides that: “Service out of the jurisdiction of a writ of summons or notice of a writ of summons may be allowed by the Court or a judge whenever … (f) Any injunction is sought as to anything to be done within the jurisdiction”… I think if the claim of the plaintiffs was put in its proper order instead of finding item (1.) an injunction, one ought to find a different claim to which this claim for an injunction would be incidental … I do not think for myself that an injunction of such a fleeting nature is the sort of injunction which is referred to or indeed to be included in sub-r. (f). Rosler v. Hilbery, [1925] 1 Ch. D. 250 (C.A.), at 258, per Pollock M.R. Proper party to action Clement J.A. in Talbot v. Pan Ocean Oil Corp. (1977), 3 Alta. L.R. (2d) 354 (C.A.), at 365, quoted with approval Lewis v. Engineering Products of Canada Ltd. (1971), 7 N.S.R. (2d) 139 (T.D.), which in turn quoted, at p. 149, Lord Esher M.R. in Massey v. Heynes & Co. (1888), 21 Q.B.D. 330 (C.A.): The question, whether a person out of the jurisdiction is a ‘proper party’ to an action against a person who has been served within the jurisdiction, must depend on this—supposing both parties had been within the jurisdiction, would they both have been proper parties to the action? If they would, and only one of them is in this country, then the rule says that the other may be served, just as if he had been within the jurisdiction. Cowan C.J.T.D. in Lewis went on to quote Williston and Rolls, The Law of Civil Procedure, and this is again referred to by Clement J.A. in Talbot, at pp. 365–66: where this sub-rule applies, the court assumes jurisdiction to entertain an action against a person over whom it would otherwise have no jurisdiction, if the action had been brought against him alone. Leave for service out of the jurisdiction may be given in cases where leave could not be granted under any of the other sub-rules, for example, a tort committed outside the jurisdiction, subject to three conditions—(1) that the action must be properly brought against the defendant within the province; (2) the original defendant must be served within the province before an order can be made under the sub-rule and (3) the person out of the province must be a necessary or proper party to the action, and, in this case, as indicated in Massey v. Heynes & Co., supra, the words are alternative. A person may be a ‘proper’ party even though he is not a ‘necessary’ party. In Klondike Helicopters v. Fairchild Republic Co. (1979), 8 Alta. L.R. (2d) 396 (T.D.), at 400, MacDonald J. quoted with approval Kekewich J. in Collins v. North British & Mercantile Insurance Co., [1894] 3 Ch. D. 228 at 236 as to the meaning of the words “proper party”: Those words must refer to the action in which the defendant is a necessary and proper party, not to another action, and you cannot make it the same action by putting it into the same suit. It cannot be the meaning of the rule that you can make A and B parties and ask one relief against A and another against B, and say because you have a good cause of action against A, therefore you can join B, who is a party out of the jurisdiction, seeking relief against him on another cause of action against him. If more than one defendant is named, the defendants within the jurisdiction must be served before one may properly seek leave to serve the defendants outside the jurisdiction. Clearly the plaintiff cannot support the service under (g) [the equivalent to Alberta's R. 30(j)] as the defendant company, the only defendant within the jurisdiction, had not been served when the statement of claim was served on the defendant [out of the jurisdiction]…Goodbun v. McRae[1927] 2 W.W.R. 216 (Man. C.A.), at 218, per Fullerton J.A.
