sentences.text: Commentary § 11.25:1 Rule 11.25 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
Overview In Ayles v.
Arsenault, 2011 ABQB 493, 2011 CarswellAlta 1416, 523 A.R.
L.R.

(5th) 131, Justice Browne gave the following overview of the law relating to the court taking jurisdiction over an out-of-province defendant (at paragraphs 15–20): 15 Section 11.25(3) enumerates a number of circumstances where a real and substantial connection is presumed to exist.
Those circumstances are set out above but none apply to the facts that are before the Court in this action.

16 Regardless of whether one of the circumstances provided for in the rules is satisfied, a Court cannot take jurisdiction over an out-of-province defendant unless the test for real and substantial connection is met: Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Co. of Canada v.
Wainoco Oil & Gas Co., 2004 ABQB 643, 364 A.R.
151 at para.

Although Rule 11.25(3) is not exhaustive of the circumstances that may establish a real and substantial connection between the Province and the facts on which the claim in the action is based, in the absence of one of the enumerated circumstances applying, as here, the onus is on the Plaintiff to establish a real and substantial connection.
17 The question of whether this Court has jurisdiction over this action involves a two-stage inquiry: Royal & Sun Alliance at paras.
Can this Court exercise jurisdiction simpliciter over this action on the basis of a real and substantial connection?
If so, should this Court exercise jurisdiction over this action in light of the doctrine of forum non conveniens?

18 The second stage of the inquiry recognizes that even where a Court can properly assume jurisdiction over an action under the first stage, it retains the residual discretion to decline to exercise its jurisdiction on the grounds that it is forum non conveniens and that there exists a more appropriate forum in which to entertain the action: Muscutt v.
Courcelles (2002), 60 O.R.
(3d) 20, 2002 CarswellOnt 1756 at para.
40 (C.A.); Royal & Sun Alliance at para.
19 Of significance is that the first and second stages of the inquiry are distinct.
Sharpe J.A. provides the following assistance in Muscutt at para.
43: While the real and substantial connection test is a legal rule, the forum non conveniens test is discretionary.
The real and substantial connection test involves a fact-specific inquiry, but the test ultimately rests upon legal principles of general application.

The question is whether the forum can assume jurisdiction over the claims of plaintiffs in general against defendants in general given the sort of relationship between the case, the parties and the forum.
By contrast, the forum non conveniens test is a discretionary test that focuses upon the particular facts of the parties and the case.
The question is whether the forum should assert jurisdiction at the suit of this particular plaintiff against this particular defendant.

20 The doctrine of forum non conveniens is to be considered separate from and subsequent to the issue of real and substantial connection under the first stage, and it only arises where more than one forum can properly take jurisdiction simpliciter.
If this Court does not have jurisdiction over this matter, the issue of the convenience of the forum is irrelevant: Royal & Sun Alliance at paras.

Moreover, “the factors listed for consideration at the second, discretionary, forum non conveniens stage, have no bearing on real and substantial connection and, therefore, should not be considered at the first stage of jurisdiction simpliciter analysis”: Van Breda v.
Village Resorts Ltd., 2010 ONCA 84, 98 O.R.
(3d) 721 at para.
In Sears Canada Inc. v.

C & S Interior Designs Ltd., 2012 ABQB 573, Madam Justice Kent said, at paragraphs 12–17: 12 The Supreme Court of Canada recently clarified the Canadian choice of forum test for disputes over jurisdiction in Club Resorts Ltd. v.
Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17 (“Van Breda”). … 13 The test consists of two components.
The first is the jurisdiction simpliciter component, which asks whether sufficient grounds exist upon which a court can assume jurisdiction.

The second is the forum non conveniens component, which asks, given the existence of at least two possible jurisdictions, whether a court should exercise its discretion and assume jurisdiction over the matter.
14 In Van Breda the Supreme Court adopted an objective approach to determining the jurisdiction simplicter question using presumptive connecting factors.
The party arguing for the assumption of jurisdiction must be able to point to a factor that presumptively indicates a real and substantial connection between the dispute and that jurisdiction.

Justice LeBel, speaking for a unanimous Court, stated: [90] To recap, in a case concerning a tort, the following factors are presumptive connecting factors that, prima facie, entitle a court to assume jurisdiction over a dispute:
(a) the defendant is domiciled or resident in the province
(b) the defendant carries on business in the province
(c) the tort was committed in the province; and
(d) a contract connected with the dispute was made in the province.
While the Supreme Court did not expressly extend this reasoning to contractual disputes, there appears to be no reason that they cannot be applied more generally.
15 Furthermore, this list of presumptive factors is open to expansion.
LeBel J went on to state: [91] As I mentioned above, the list of presumptive connecting factors is not closed.
Over time, courts may identify new factors which also presumptively entitle a court to assume jurisdiction.
In identifying new presumptive factors, a court should look to connections that give rise to a relationship with the forum that is similar in nature to the ones which result from the listed factors.
Relevant considerations include:
(a) Similarity of the connecting factor with the recognized presumptive connecting factors
(b) Treatment of the connecting factor in the case law
(c) Treatment of the connecting factor in statute law; and
(d) Treatment of the connecting factor in the private international law of other legal systems with a shared commitment to order, fairness and comity.

[92] When a court considers whether a new connecting factor should be given presumptive effect, the values of order, fairness and comity can serve as useful analytical tools for assessing the strength of the relationship with a forum to which the factor in question points.
These values underlie all presumptive connecting factors, whether listed or new.

All presumptive connecting factors generally point to a relationship between the subject matter of the litigation and the forum such that it would be reasonable to expect that the defendant would be called to answer legal proceedings in that forum.

Where such a relationship exists, one would generally expect Canadian courts to recognize and enforce a foreign judgment on the basis of the presumptive connecting factor in question, and foreign courts could be expected to do the same with respect to Canadian judgments.
The assumption of jurisdiction would thus appear to be consistent with the principles of comity, order and fairness.
After the existence of a presumptive connecting factor has been established, it is open to the challenging party to rebut the presumption on the facts.

If presumptive factors are lacking, or are successfully rebutted, the court must dismiss or stay the action, subject to the possible application of the forum of necessity doctrine (not an issue in the present case).
Likewise, once a presumptive factor is established, and no rebuttals are successful, the court must exercise its jurisdiction, unless the defendant invokes forum non conveniens.
16 In order to raise a forum non coneniens argument, a defendant must first establish that another jurisdiction has jurisdiction simpliciter using that same test.
It is then within the discretion of the court to refuse jurisdiction if the defendant is able to show that it would be fairer and more efficient to have the matter adjudicated elsewhere.
17 The court should be flexible in its consideration of the facts at this stage.
They may be different from case-to-case and from province-to-province.
In Van Breda, LeBel J noted at para 105: Despite some legislative attempts to draw up exhaustive lists, I doubt that it will ever be possible to do so.

In essence, the doctrine [focuses] on the contexts of individual cases, and its purpose is to ensure that both parties are treated fairly and that the process for resolving their litigation is efficient.
The factors cited in Master Hanebury's decision as summarized in Norex Petroleum Ltd. v.
Chubb Insurance Co of Canada, 2008 ABQB 442 at para 93, (2009), 444 AR 102, may be taken as the guiding standard in Alberta.
For ease of reference I list them here:
(1) where each party resides
(2) where each party carries on business
(3) where the cause of action arose
(4) where the loss or damage occurred
(5) any juridical advantage for the plaintiff in this jurisdiction
(6) any juridical disadvantage for the defendant in this jurisdiction
(7) convenience or inconvenience to potential witnesses
(8) the cost of conducting the litigation in this jurisdiction
(9) applicable substantive law; and
(10) difficulty in proving foreign law, if necessary.
These factors should be considered together and weighed holistically, in accordance with the flexibility and discretion granted to courts at this stage.
Rule is mandatory In Osadchuk v.

Kidd, 2024 ABKB 448, Justice Simard said: [20] … The introductory language in Rule 11.25(2) states clearly that “A commencement document may be served outside Canada only if” the requirements in the Rule are met.
The requirements of the Rule are mandatory.

If the requirements were not met, the Claims could not be served outside Canada. … [28] In a similar vein, Justice Nixon of this Court recently stated that the Rules governing the service of documents outside Alberta must be construed strictly, and if the mandatory requirements in Rule 11.25 are not complied with, the Court cannot later validate service under Rule 1.5 or Rule 11.27: Ball v 1979927 Alberta Ltd, 2022 ABKB 814 at paras 31- 33.
Serving a commencement document outside Alberta but within Canada In Greenbuilt Group of Companies Ltd. v.
RMD Engineering Inc., 2013 ABQB 297, 2013 CarswellAlta 806, 563 A.R.
1, 82 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 349, Justice Wakeling provided a detailed summary of the law regarding service ex juris.
His Lordship reviewed the development of the law, and the differences between the previous Rules and the current Rules.
At paragraphs 94–101, 103-104, Wakeling, J.
(as he then was) set out the questions which a Court must answer when determining the validity of extraterritorial service of a commencement document within Canada.
He said: 94 The new service ex juris rules jettisoned past practice.
There is no longer the need to secure prior judicial permission to serve a commencement document extraterritorially within Canada.

By deleting the merit based component for service outside of Alberta but within Canada, the new rules shine a bright light on one important issue—does the court have jurisdiction to hear the plaintiff's claim?
95 These are significant changes.

3. — The Principled Approach to the Service Ex Juris and Jurisdiction Questions 96 There are a number of straightforward and uncomplicated steps which this Court must complete to properly assess a challenge to the validity of the extraterritorial service of its process within Canada.

97 At the outset, the Court must refer to the commencement document and any material filed in support of and in opposition to a rule 11.31(1) set-aside application to collect the factual assertions which must be evaluated to determine whether “a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based”, the test recorded in rule 11.25(1)(a) of the new rules.
Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v.
Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd., 440 A.R.
2009)(the court reviewed the pleadings, affidavits filed in support of and in opposition to a set-aside motion and cross-examination on affidavits) &Horni A Hutni Tezirstvo v.
Kosner, [1951] A.C.
869, 884 (H.L.) (“There is voluminous affidavit evidence on both sides”).
A defendant must take care not to supply any factual assertions which may assist the plaintiff.
This is not an uncommon error.
Chemische Fabrik Vormals Sandoz v.
Badische Anilin und Soda Fabriks, 90 L.T.
1904)(the affidavits filed by the party moving to set aside service outside the United Kingdom filled in the gaps in the plaintiff's original supporting affidavit).
98 Next, the Court must ask three questions.

99 First, are there factual assertions within the pool of factual assertions collected by the first step which demonstrate that “a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based”?
This standard appears in rule 11.25(1)(a).
It is important to recall that the focus is on factual assertions or allegations.
This is not the stage of the litigation continuum where findings of fact are made.
That is the role of the trial court, a task discharged with full exposure to the work product of the full litigation continuum.
Vitkovice Horni A Hutni Tezirstvo v.
Kosner, [1951] A.C.
869, 879 (H.L.)(it is not “the duty of the court … to try the action upon the preliminary application”) &Chemische Fabrik Vormals Sandoz v.
Badische Anilin und Soda Fabriks, 90 L.T.
1904)(“the court is not on an application for leave to serve out of the jurisdiction … called upon to try the action”).
100 If the factual assertions in the pool collected by the first step meet this standard, the Court has the jurisdiction to hear an action which contains these factual assertions.
It must be then determined whether the commencement document incorporates enough of the factual assertions which caused the Court to answer the preceding question positively.
This is the thrust of the second question.

101 Second, do the factual assertions in the commencement document, a subset of the factual assertions collected at the first step, disclose the “facts in support [of the real and substantial connection]”, the standard incorporated in rule 11.25(1)(b) of the new rules?
If not, the court cannot conclude that it has the jurisdiction to hear the action as currently framed.

And because the standard for establishing jurisdiction and the lawfulness of extraterritorial service are the same, it follows that a negative determination on the jurisdiction query compels a negative determination on the validity of service ex juris. … 103 Third, does the commencement document “specifically …[refer] to the grounds for service of the document outside Alberta and in Canada [set out in rule 11.25(3)]”, a requirement found in rule 11.25
A careful pleader will have expressly asserted that the plaintiff makes a claim listed in rule 11.25(3).
An omission of this critical assertion deprives the commencement document of a feature necessary to a finding that extraterritorial service is lawful.
104 One will note that no inquiry is pursued to determine whether the asserted facts disclose a “good arguable case”.
This is because a merit based question does not arise under rule 11.25(1).
In Talbott v.
Talbott, 2021 ABQB 291, 2021 CarswellAlta 959, Justice Jeffrey disagreed with the Greenbuilt decision.
His Lordship said: [11] With respect, again, I disagree.
Rule 11.25(3) itemizes “circumstances in which a real and substantial connection may exist” between Alberta and the claim's allegations of fact.
Disclosing within the commencing document the “facts in support” of that real and substantial connection is the first requirement of Rule 11.25(1)(b) and it is distinct from the second.

The first requirement of Rule 11.25(1)(b) must be satisfied by disclosure of facts in the commencing document supporting the real and substantial connection; the second requirement of Rule 11.25(1)(b) must be satisfied by specific reference to the grounds for service outside Alberta but within Canada.
[12] I consider the two to be addressing distinct requirements, not merely using different words to describe the same requirement, because:
(i) the first goes to the Court's jurisdiction, the second does not
(ii) this interpretation accords with the comparable approach in Rule 11.25(2)(a) dealing with service outside Canada.

In that situation, the Court must be satisfied that a real and substantial connection exists (which necessarily entails an applicant adducing evidence on the point) and, separately, the applicant must separately provide “a document or affidavit that sets out the grounds for service of the document outside Canada”; and

(iii) The old practice before the advent of Rule 11.25 in 2010, pursuant to then Rule 31(b), required an applicant seeking permission of the Court for service ex juris, to separately address where the party to be served might be found.

[13] I note also from the jurisprudence at that time that the Court in considering such service ex juris requests placed the paramount importance on its jurisdiction over the lis, less so on the grounds for effecting service outside the jurisdiction.
This goes to whether any deficiency in disclosing the grounds for service might be considered trivial or more critical.

[14] My point in examining the reasoning in Greenbuilt, which the Appellant relies on to say the requirement to specifically refer to the grounds for service outside Alberta is non-trivial, is that when Wakeling J speaks of “[a]n omission of this critical assertion” in Greenbuilt, he is referring to the “real and substantial connection”.
He was speaking of the lawfulness of the Court exercising jurisdiction extraterritorially (in his words: “a feature necessary to a finding that extraterritorial service is lawful”).
He was not speaking of effecting service extraterritorially.

[15] This focus is also evident at para 94 of his decision: By deleting the merit based component for service outside of Alberta but within Canada, the new rules shine a bright light on one important issue—does the court have jurisdiction to hear the plaintiff's claim?
That issue of the Court's jurisdiction to hear a matter, I agree, is critical.
It is not trivial.
But a flaw in specifically referring to the grounds for service may or may not be trivial.
Failure to serve at all a party from whom relief is claimed is not trivial; the right to be notified is a foundational principle of natural justice.
It must be satisfied before a party can access every other procedural right entailed by audi alteram partem.
[16] Referring to the grounds for service, however, is most often trivial.
It does not go to the Court's jurisdiction but to the process for notifying a person about a matter within its jurisdiction.
Other Rules accord the Court discretion to relieve or remedy flaws in modes of service.
See, for example: Rules 11.27 and 1.2 through 1.5.
Service is frequently deemed sufficient after the fact, in a broad range of circumstances.
Justice Jeffrey referred to Greenbuilt Group of Companies Ltd v.
RMD Engineering Inc., 2013 ABQB 346, 2013 CarswellAlta 1024, but the paragraphs to which his Lordship referred are in 2013 ABQB 297.
Real and Substantial Connection In Acciona Infrastructure Canada Inc. v.
Posco Daewoo Corporation, 2019 ABCA 241, 2019 CarswellAlta 1169, 91 Alta.

The forum non conveniens analysis permits a defendant to show why the court should decline to exercise its jurisdiction in favour of another forum that also has a real and substantive connection under conflicts rules, but which is a more appropriate forum to dispose of the action. … [17] In Van Breda, the Supreme Court described a non-exhaustive list of presumptive connecting factors, the existence of which allow a court to presume that the claim is properly before it under conflicts rules, absent indications to the contrary: para 80.
These are objective factors that connect the subject matter of the litigation with the forum.

For example, in a tort claim, a court would be entitled to assume jurisdiction over a dispute where: a) the defendant is domiciled or resident in the province; b) the defendant carries on business in the province; c) the tort was committed in the province; and d) a contract connected with the dispute was made in the province.
[18] As noted above, the list is not exhaustive.

In identifying new presumptive factors, a court should look to connections that “give rise to a relationship with the forum that is similar in nature to the ones which result from the listed factors”: Van Breda at para 91.
The court in Van Breda found it useful to have regard to factors drawn from the Ontario rules of civil procedure that relate to situations in which service ex juris is allowed: see para 83.

As the court noted, although these factors relate to service ex juris and were not adopted as conflicts rules, they “represent an expression of wisdom and experience drawn from the life of the law”, many “are based on objective facts that may also indicate when courts can properly assume jurisdiction”, and they can offer guidance for the development of this area of private international law.

[19] Similarly, the Alberta Rules of Court provide that document commencing an Alberta action may be served outside Alberta where “a real and substantial connection exists between Alberta and the facts on which a claim in the action is based”: Rule 11.25(1). … … [26] As was noted by LeBel J in Van Breda at para 99, it would be inefficient to have a court take jurisdiction over only one part of a claim: Would a court be limited to hearing the specific part of the case that can be directly connected with the jurisdiction?
Such a rule would breach the principles of fairness and efficiency on which the assumption of jurisdiction is based.
The purpose of the conflicts rules is to establish whether a real and substantial connection exists between the forum, the subject matter of the litigation and the defendant.
If such a connection exists in respect of a factual and legal situation, the court must assume jurisdiction over all aspects of the case.
The plaintiff should not be obliged to litigate a tort claim in Manitoba and a related claim for restitution in Nova Scotia.
That would be incompatible with any notion of fairness and efficiency.

Rebutting the presumption of jurisdiction [27] The presumption of jurisdiction simplicter can be rebutted where the defendant (here, the Deadmans) establishes facts which demonstrate that the presumptive connecting factors do not point to any real relationship, or only a weak relationship, between the subject matter of the litigation and the forum. “In order for a defendant to succeed in showing that ‘a given connection is inappropriate in the circumstances of the case’ the circumstances must demonstrate that the relationship between the forum and the subject matter of the litigation is such that it would ‘not be reasonable to expect that the defendant would be called to answer proceedings in that jurisdiction’”: Haaretz.com In Nexen Energy ULC v.
ITP SA, 2020 ABQB 83, 2020 CarswellAlta 213, Mr.
Justice Nixon explained the difference between “jurisdiction simpliciter” and “forum non conveniens”: [184] The jurisdiction simpliciter analysis is meant to ensure that a court has authority.
This will be the case where a “substantial connection between the dispute and the forum” is found to exist: Barer v Knight Brothers LLC, 2019 SCC 13 at para 85.

The constitutional purpose of the jurisdiction simpliciter test is to establish a minimum threshold for the assumption of jurisdiction in order to prevent improper assumptions of jurisdiction: Haaretz.com v Goldhar, 2018 SCC 28 at para 30; see also Van Breda at para 26; and Hunt v T&N plc, 1993 CanLII 43 (SCC), [1993] 4 SCR 289, at 325.
[185] The objective of the jurisdiction simpliciter test is to delineate circumstances in which a court has jurisdiction.
The jurisdiction simpliciter test is not to delineate circumstances in which a court should exercise jurisdiction.
That is the purpose of forum non conveniens.
[186] The prioritization of order and predictability at the jurisdiction simpliciter stage is also consistent with the principle of comity.
That principle is central to Canadian private international law: Haaretz.com at para 30; and Van Breda at para 74.

[187] On the other hand, the forum non conveniens analysis is to guide a court in deciding whether it should decline to exercise that jurisdiction in favour of a forum that is “clearly more appropriate”: Haaretz.com at para 28; see also Van Breda at paras 46 and 56, affirming the reasoning of Sharpe JA in Muscutt v Courcelles
(4th) 577 (ONCA); and Van Breda v Village Resorts Ltd, 2010 ONCA 84.
In Sports Corp. v.
Svoboda, 2004 ABQB 450, 2004 CarswellAlta 823, 362 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 143, Hillier J. discussed the test to be applied when determining whether an order for service ex juris should be granted.
After noting the difference between a test based on “real and substantial connection” and a test based on a “good arguable case”, his Lordship said, at pp.
279–280: Deuruneft Deutsche-Russische Mineralol Handelsgesellschaft mbH v.
Bullen (2003), 349 A.R.
221 (Q.B.), dealt with two applications, one regarding forum conveniens and one to set aside an order for service ex juris.
After clearly distinguishing the concepts of forum conveniens and service ex juris, Justice McMahon (para.

27) addresses the test applicable to jurisdiction: In order for this Court to assert jurisdiction over the Counterclaim a real and substantial connection must be demonstrated between it and the Counterclaim.
If such a connection can be shown, and jurisdiction simpliciter is established, the Court must further consider whether it should decline jurisdiction in favour of a more convenient forum.
Put another way, the first inquiry is whether the Court can exercise jurisdiction and the second is whether it should.
Justice McMahon suggests that perhaps a more onerous test is required for international disputes, but goes on to adopt and apply the real and substantial connection test.
McMahon J. notes (para.

47) that the Supreme Court of Canada has not defined what constitutes a real and substantial connection, but holds that the assumption of jurisdiction must be founded upon the requirements of order and fairness, rather than a mechanical counting of contacts or connections.
The Court then applies the eight factors from Muscett et al. v.
Courcelles et al.
(3d) 20 (C.A.) to determine if there is a real and substantial connection:
(1) the connection between the forum and the plaintiff's claim, because a forum has an interest in protecting the legal rights of its residents

(2) a connection between the forum and the defendant, which may occur where it was reasonably foreseeable that the defendant's conduct would result in harm within the jurisdiction or where the defendant has done something within the jurisdiction that bears upon the plaintiff's claim
(3) unfairness to the defendant in assuming jurisdiction
(4) unfairness to the plaintiff in not assuming jurisdiction
(5) the involvement of other parties to the suit, which factor included concerns about avoiding a multiplicity of proceedings and the risk of inconsistent results
(6) the court's willingness to recognize and enforce an extra-provincial judgment rendered on the same jurisdictional basis
(7) whether the case is inter-provincial or international in nature, because the assumption of jurisdiction is more easily justified in inter-provincial cases; and
(8) comity and the standards of jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement prevailing elsewhere.

Having assessed the import of these decisions, I am able to conclude that it is not so much the label or terminology of a singular test to be applied; rather, the objective is to conduct a fair and proper assessment of the claim and the parties to determine a definite connection to Alberta.
For the purposes of this application, it is unnecessary to decide whether the same or higher evidentiary standard would apply in cases of forum conveniens or foreign judgment enforcement.

Without deciding whether the test for service ex juris may only be expressed and applied according to a “real and substantial” standard, I interpret that terminology as a reasonable and accurate description of the flexible, fair link to be shown by [the plaintiff] at this stage.
Justice Brooker in Norex Petroleum Ltd. v.
Chubb Insurance Co. of Canada (2008), 95 Alta.
L.R.

(4th) 74 (Q.B.) (a case involving a contractual dispute between a Russian company and a Canadian company over a contract executed in Russia and dealing with Russian property) thoroughly reviewed the above factors in relation to forum conveniens.

An interesting aspect of his analysis is that, on the evidence before him, his Lordship found, under the factor “any juridical advantage for the plaintiff in this [Alberta] jurisdiction”, that Alberta was the preferable forum for the litigation because of concerns about corruption in the Russian courts.
Who Bears the Onus?
In Cybersurf Corp. v.
Mercury Partners & Co.
110 (Q.B.), the Applicant sought an order setting aside an ex parte order for service ex juris.
Madam Justice Rawlins discussed the issue of which party bears the onus to show that Alberta is the forum conveniens.
At pp.
115, her Ladyship said: United Oilseed[United Oilseed Products Ltd. v.
Royal Bank of Canada (1988), 87 A.R.
337 (Alta.

C.A.)] stands for the proposition that where jurisdiction does not exist as of right, the party seeking to establish jurisdiction must demonstrate that there is no other available forum which is clearly or distinctly more suitable.
Jurisdiction will exist as a right where the defendant is a resident in the jurisdiction.
Accordingly, the onus here would appear to be on the Respondent to demonstrate that this is clearly the most appropriate forum.
However, in Amchem, [Amchem Products Inc. et al. v.
Workers Compensation Board (1993), 102 D.L.R.
(4th) 96 (S.C.C.)] the Supreme Court of Canada found at p.
111: “Whether the burden of proof should be on the plaintiff in ex juris cases will depend on the rule that permits service out of the jurisdiction.

If it requires that service out of the jurisdiction be justified by the plaintiff, whether on an application for an order or in defending service ex juris where no order is required, then the rule must govern.

The burden of proof should not play a significant role in these matters as it only applies in cases in which the judge cannot come to a determinate decision on the basis of the material presented by the parties.

While the standard remains that applicable in civil cases I agree with the English authorities that the existence of a more appropriate forum must be clearly established to displace the forum selected by the plaintiff.” (Emphasis added.) Kenny, J., in Direct Energy Marketing Ltd. v.
Hillson (1999), 247 A.R.
48 (Q.B.), considered these two decisions in circumstances similar to those here.
In Direct Energy the Defendant, a Saskatchewan resident, applied to have the order allowing him to be served ex juris set aside on the basis that Alberta was not the forum conveniens.

There, Kenny, J., found that, as leave to serve ex juris is still required in Alberta (Rules 30 and 31), the Supreme Court of Canada's comments in Amchem on forum conveniens should not be taken as overruling United Oilseed.
She relied on J.G.

Castel, Canadian Conflict of Laws (Butterworths: Vancouver, 1997), in this regard, wherein the author notes: In provinces where leave to serve the defendant ex juris is always required [and there is a footnote here to Alberta and Newfoundland and specifically the United Oilseed case], the Plaintiff must show affirmatively that the local forum is clearly more appropriate than any other forum.

Kenny, J., concluded in the case before her: I will proceed to consider the question on the basis of the material provided by Counsel and only if I am unable to reach a decision on that will [the plaintiff's] arguments as to the burden of proof become critical.
However, I am satisfied in light of the authorities that [the plaintiff] does bear the onus of establishing Alberta as the forum conveniens.
I propose to deal with this application on the same basis.
Namely, I find that the onus here lies on the Respondent, however, I will only have resort to it if I am otherwise unable to determine the forum conveniens.
In Gulevich v.

Miller, 2015 ABCA 411, Justice Watson said: 18 It is the plaintiff's onus to establish that a presumptive connecting factor to the plaintiff's chosen jurisdiction exists and the defendant's onus to rebut the presumption: Van Breda and its companion case, Éditions Écosociété Inc. v Banro Corp., 2012 SCC 18, [2012] 1 SCR 636.
In those cases the plaintiff sued in its preferred jurisdiction and the defendants applied for a declaration that the plaintiff's preferred jurisdiction lacked a “real and substantial connection”.

If successful, “the court might presume, absent indications to the contrary, that the claim is properly before it under the conflicts rules and that it is acting within the limits of its constitutional jurisdiction”: Van Breda at para 80.

Said another way, the “party arguing that the court should assume jurisdiction has the burden of identifying a presumptive connecting factor that links the subject matter of the litigation to the forum”: Van Breda at para 100.
19 The appellants pleaded “the claim relates to a tort committed in Alberta” which requires them to discharge the burden.

If successful, “the burden of rebutting [the presumption that Alberta is the proper forum] rests on the party challenging the assumption of jurisdiction”, here the respondent doctor: Van Breda at para 99.

The defendant can rebut the presumption by showing that the “presumptive factor does not point to any real relationship between the subject matter of the litigation and the forum or points only to a weak relationship between them.”: para 95.
Good Arguable Case (a)—Under the New Rules In Scott & Associates Engineering Ltd. v.
Ghost Pine Windfarm, LP, 2011 ABQB 630, 2011 CarswellAlta 1911, 520 A.R.
L.R.
(5th) 357; additional reasons at 2012 ABQB 26, 2012 CarswellAlta 272, 534 A.R.
75, 66 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 207 (Q.B.) Chief Justice Wittmann discussed whether the concept of a “good arguable case” as it was developed under the old Rules applies to the new Rules.
He held that it does.

At paragraphs 30, 32–34, 39–40, his Lordship said: 30 The position of SAEL is that there is no requirement for a “good arguable case” under the New ARC and that therefore, it need not establish a good arguable case in order to successfully resist an application to set aside the ex-juris orders, because the New ARC apply. … 32 I apprehend the position adopted in Alberta, taken from Vikpovice, is that the standard of proof to be attained to support service ex-juris, in terms of establishing that a plaintiff “has a reasonable cause of action” as set forth in Old ARC 31(a) is somewhat elusive.
Recognizing the difficulty of a plaintiff in attaining the same standard of proof as would be necessary in a trial, the standard is less.
That standard is simply an assessment of the particular facts of the case in terms of whether it is good and arguable.
33 But what does that mean?
Some assistance is gained from Vikpovice itself in the judgment of Lord Simonds, where he said at [1951] 2 All E.R.
334 at 338: It is, no doubt, difficult to say precisely what test must be passed for an applicant to make it sufficiently appear that the case is a proper one.
I do not wholly like the expression a “prima facie case”, for where leave to serve has been given ex parte under Ord.
11 and application is then made under Ord.

12 to set the proceedings aside, a conflict may arise in which the question is not so much whether a prima facie case has been made out as whether upon all the materials then before him, the judge is of opinion that the case—I can find no better word—is a proper one to be heard in our courts.
The description “a good arguable case” has been suggested and I do not quarrel with it.” 34 Under the Old ARC, what did “good arguable case” mean?

In my view, it meant a case that was not fanciful or speculative but was grounded upon some evidence upon which an objective trier would say “well, on the basis of the facts presented, the case is arguable and certainly is not to be dismissed out of hand.” … 39 For this court to do away with the good arguable case criterion and have no standard whatsoever, which is what SAEL asserts, would in my view require that under the New ARC there should be express or implied a provision that a “good arguable case” is not required to be made out to support valid service outside of Canada pursuant to Rule 11.25(2).
It is common ground that there is no express exclusion of the requirement in the New ARC.
Nor is anything to be implied from the New ARC which would do away with this requirement.
40 Logic and common sense dictate some standard of proof in addition to mere allegations in a statement of claim in order to support service of an originating document outside of the jurisdiction.
Were it otherwise, this Court could take jurisdiction over any person or entity outside the jurisdiction solely on the basis of unproven allegations in an originating document.
That has never been the law and would give rise to a potential for much mischief should it become so.
Thus, to resolve the issue in this case, namely whether the ex-juris orders ought to be set aside, I continue the requirement of a good arguable case, which requires some evidence ….

(b)—Under the Old Rules The requirement of a “good arguable case”—as the test of whether a defendant is “a proper or necessary party to an action properly brought against another person served within Alberta”—is satisfied where the material filed supports the causes of action pleaded; where all the defendants are or may be involved in any of these causes of action.

In short, where the facts alleged establish that a defendant exhibits a “definite connection” to the case, the requirement of a “good arguable case” is met and that defendant is a proper or necessary party.
Suncor Inc. v.
Canada Wire & Cable Ltd.

And Fraser C.J.A. said: We are satisfied that the affidavit evidence and the other evidence adduced is sufficient to raise what the relevant authorities describe as permitting an order for service ex juris, that is a “good arguable case”.
The law does not require that the Appellants establish a winning case as a condition precedent to securing an order for service ex juris.
As noted in Nova, an Alberta Corp. v.
Grove, [22 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 262 (C.A.)], only prima facie evidence is needed and the standard of proof is lax at this stage.
Cunningham v.
Hamilton (1995), 29 Alta.
L.R.
In Osadchuk v.

Kidd, 2024 ABKB 448, Justice Simard said: [17] Alberta courts have consistently held that there is an additional requirement to obtain a service ex juris order that is not expressly stated in Rule 11.25(2): the applicant must also show that it has a “good arguable case”: Acciona Infrastructure Canada Inc v Posco Daewoo Corporation, 2019 ABCA 241 at para 14.

As explained by Dilts J in 801 Seventh Inc v CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC, 2020 ABQB 198 at para 33: “[t]he requirement to establish a good arguable case does not require evidence of every cause of action, but sufficient evidence for the court to determine that it should assume jurisdiction over the party and the dispute.” 8.
Standard of Proof The standard of proof in service ex juris applications was also recently discussed by the Alberta Court of Appeal in Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v.
Stearns Catalytic Ltd.
No.
11672, 11673 and 11675 (unreported).
In the context of a motion to set aside service ex juris, the court stated that: Rule 31 and the binding cases under it set a fairly lax standard of proof, and for good reason.
In particular, they do not call for first-hand knowledge, a positive factual conclusion, or evidence excluding possible defences.
Suncor Inc. v.
Canada Wire & Cable Ltd.
Tort Committed in Alberta—Statement versus Inference It is true that the affidavit nowhere expressly said that the tort was committed in Alberta, but it strongly implied that in several places.
There are various plaintiffs, all sworn to be Alberta residents, and it is shown that the misrepresentations from the defendants were put into the media, including the Wall Street Journal.
So it scarcely seems likely that over the short period of time the several plaintiffs all happened to go to the United States and there receive the misrepresentation.
And it is common ground that a tort is committed where the victim receives (hears) the misrepresentation.
The only reasonable conclusion, which the chambers judge obviously drew, was that there was prima facie evidence that occurred in Alberta.
Paterson v.
Hamilton (1991), 79 Alta.
L.R.
Lifting the Corporate Veil In an application to set aside a refusal to grant an order for service ex juris, the Court of Appeal, speaking through Fraser C.J.A., in Cunningham v.
Hamilton (1995), 29 Alta.
L.R.

(3d) 380, at 382–83, said: The sole basis of the Appellants' arguments rests on the proposition that BHP was, at the time of the merger between it and Hamilton Oil Corporation (“HOC”), the alter ego of Broken Hill or vice versa.
Hence, contends the appellants, the corporate veil should be lifted and the Court should treat Broken Hill as the true successor corporation to HOC.
We do not agree.
It is true that Broken Hill operates a number of its worldwide companies as an integrated economic unit.
But the mere fact that it does so does not mean that for legal purposes, separate legal entities will be ignored absent some compelling reason for lifting the corporate veil.
As noted in Adams v.
Cape Industries plc, [1990] Ch.
433 (C.A.), at 536, citing Goff L.J. in Bank of Tokyo Ltd. v.
Karoon (Note) (1986), [1987] A.C.
45: [Counsel] suggested … that it would be technical for us to distinguish between parent and subsidiary company in this context; economically, he said, they were one.
But we are concerned not with economics but with law.
The distinction between the two is, in law, fundamental and cannot here be bridged.
In other words, in my opinion the expression “affecting land” is descriptive of the obligation or liability sought to be enforced, and has no reference to the relief or remedy sought in the action.
Wilkie v.
Smith, [1944] 1 D.L.R.
224 (Sask.
C.A.), at 225, per MacDonald J.A. and quoted with approval in Kroll Associates Inc. v.
Calvi (1998), 60 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 135 (Q.B.), at 142, per Kenny J.
The defendant must be ordinarily resident in Alberta at the time the action is commenced: Finnerty v.
Watson, [1969] 1 O.R.
Although this is an Ontario case, the principle is the same and confirms what the rule purports to state.
In Alberta, Master Funduk has said: Subrule (c) is essentially the common law rule that the local court has in personam jurisdiction over persons who are domiciled or ordinarily resident here.
Hanson v.
E & D Aircraft Services Ltd.
120 at 123 (Master).
Tort action The fact that the tort is alleged to have occurred in Alberta and other provinces, does not take the action outside R.
30(h), As is alleged in the claim the publication was made by means of television by the defendant Corporation whose network extends throughout Canada.
Does the fact that such publication occurred in other jurisdictions than Alberta preclude ex juris for this alleged tort which occurred in Alberta among other jurisdictions?
I think not.

The plaintiff in alleging other jurisdictions in addition to Alberta is merely stating the plain facts and to delete other jurisdictions from the Statement of Claim would not be in accord with the actual facts.
U.A., Local 488 v.
Canadian Broadcasting Corp.
Often a tort arises as a result of a number of events.
To determine where the tort arose for the purposes of R.
30(h), Lawton L.J. stated: … I look back over the series of events alleged to constitute the tort and ask myself the question: where in substance did this cause of action arise?
Multinational Gas & Petrochemical Co. v.
Multinational Gas & Petrochemical Services, [1983] 2 All E.R.
In the same case, at p.
582, Dillon L.J. put the question this way: … where was the wrongful act, from which the damage flows, in fact done?
The place where the damage occurs is not determinative.
In a negligence case the happening of damage to the plaintiff is a necessary ingredient in the cause of action, and it is the last event completing the cause of action.

But the place where it happens may be quite fortuitous and should not by itself be the sole determinant of jurisdiction … It is not the right approach to say that, because there was no complete tort until the damage occurred, therefore the cause of action arose whenever the damage happened to occur.
The right approach is, when the tort is complete, to look back over the series of events constituting it and ask the question: where in substance did this cause of action arise?
Distillers Co.
(Biochemicals) v.
Thompson, [1971] 1 All E.R.
Distillers was followed by the Supreme Court of Canada in Moran v.
Pyle National (Canada) Ltd., [1975] 1 S.C.R.
Injunctive relief The injunctive relief sought must not be incidental to the action.
Rule 1 provides that: “Service out of the jurisdiction of a writ of summons or notice of a writ of summons may be allowed by the Court or a judge whenever …

(f) Any injunction is sought as to anything to be done within the jurisdiction”… I think if the claim of the plaintiffs was put in its proper order instead of finding item (1.) an injunction, one ought to find a different claim to which this claim for an injunction would be incidental … I do not think for myself that an injunction of such a fleeting nature is the sort of injunction which is referred to or indeed to be included in sub-r.
Rosler v.
Hilbery, [1925] 1 Ch.
D.
250 (C.A.), at 258, per Pollock M.R.
Proper party to action Clement J.A. in Talbot v.
Pan Ocean Oil Corp.
L.R.
(2d) 354 (C.A.), at 365, quoted with approval Lewis v.
Engineering Products of Canada Ltd.
(2d) 139 (T.D.), which in turn quoted, at p.
149, Lord Esher M.R. in Massey v.
Heynes & Co.

330 (C.A.): The question, whether a person out of the jurisdiction is a ‘proper party’ to an action against a person who has been served within the jurisdiction, must depend on this—supposing both parties had been within the jurisdiction, would they both have been proper parties to the action?
If they would, and only one of them is in this country, then the rule says that the other may be served, just as if he had been within the jurisdiction.
Cowan C.J.T.D. in Lewis went on to quote Williston and Rolls, The Law of Civil Procedure, and this is again referred to by Clement J.A. in Talbot, at pp.

365–66: where this sub-rule applies, the court assumes jurisdiction to entertain an action against a person over whom it would otherwise have no jurisdiction, if the action had been brought against him alone.

Leave for service out of the jurisdiction may be given in cases where leave could not be granted under any of the other sub-rules, for example, a tort committed outside the jurisdiction, subject to three conditions—(1) that the action must be properly brought against the defendant within the province
(2) the original defendant must be served within the province before an order can be made under the sub-rule and
(3) the person out of the province must be a necessary or proper party to the action, and, in this case, as indicated in Massey v.
Heynes & Co., supra, the words are alternative.
A person may be a ‘proper’ party even though he is not a ‘necessary’ party.
In Klondike Helicopters v.
Fairchild Republic Co.
L.R.
(2d) 396 (T.D.), at 400, MacDonald J. quoted with approval Kekewich J. in Collins v.
North British & Mercantile Insurance Co., [1894] 3 Ch.
D.

228 at 236 as to the meaning of the words “proper party”: Those words must refer to the action in which the defendant is a necessary and proper party, not to another action, and you cannot make it the same action by putting it into the same suit.

It cannot be the meaning of the rule that you can make A and B parties and ask one relief against A and another against B, and say because you have a good cause of action against A, therefore you can join B, who is a party out of the jurisdiction, seeking relief against him on another cause of action against him.
If more than one defendant is named, the defendants within the jurisdiction must be served before one may properly seek leave to serve the defendants outside the jurisdiction.
Clearly the plaintiff cannot support the service under (g) [the equivalent to Alberta's R.
30(j)] as the defendant company, the only defendant within the jurisdiction, had not been served when the statement of claim was served on the defendant [out of the jurisdiction]…Goodbun v.
McRae[1927] 2 W.W.R.
C.A.), at 218, per Fullerton J.A.

sentences.text: Method of service outside Alberta

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrule (2), unless the Court otherwise orders, if a document may be served outside Alberta under these rules, the document must be served (a) by a method provided by these rules for service of the document in Alberta, or (b) in accordance with the law of the jurisdiction in which the person to be served is located. (2) Where a document is to be served in a jurisdiction to which the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters applies, the document must be served in accordance with Division 8. (3) Service under subrule (1) is effected (a) if the document is served under subrule (1)(a), on the date specified by these rules for when service is effected, or (b) if the document is served under subrule (1)(b), in accordance with the law of the jurisdiction in which the person is served. (4) Service under subrule (2) is effected on the date service is effected under the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.26:1 Rule 11.26 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.26. See App. IX, infra, The Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters. 1. Service pursuant to the Hague Convention In Metcalfe Estate v. Yamaha Motor Powered Products Co., 2012 ABCA 240, 2012 CarswellAlta 1756, 536 A.R. 67, 68 Alta. L.R. (5th) 23, 26 C.P.C. (7th) 18, [2012] 12 W.W.R. 425, [2012] A.J. No. 919, the plaintiffs had obtained an order for service ex juris. The order said: “The Plaintiffs are given leave to serve ex juris a copy of the filed Statement of Claim, together with a copy of this Order, upon the Defendant … pursuant to the Article of the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad Judicial and Extra-judicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters”. The Court of Appeal held that the service effected did not comply with the Hague Convention (see: paragraph 30), and that the service ex juris order did not permit service by any other method (see: paragraphs 27, 29, 30). The Court of Appeal then discussed service under the Hague Convention. Justice J.D.B. McDonald, speaking for himself and Justice Bielby, said, at paragraphs 31–42: 31 The Hague Convention prescribes service through one of several specified methods. It does not allow service by any method other than the options identified within the Hague Convention itself. It affords flexibility only to the extent that one of the permitted options is to serve through any alternate method agreed upon between the Province of Alberta and Japan but there was no evidence that any such agreement existed or, if it existed, would authorize the service method attempted here. Therefore, domestic service law does not apply once the Hague Convention is engaged by the terms of a service order. 32 The Hague Convention provides a mechanism by which documents in civil and commercial disputes among private litigants can be served in different countries. The Hague Convention requires each contracting state to establish a Central Authority to receive requests for service of documents from other countries. In Canada, each province and territory has a Central Authority2. Once a Central Authority receives a request, it must serve the documents as prescribed by the internal law of the receiving state, or as designated by the requester and compatible with the law of the receiving state. Service can also be effected by a party as otherwise expressly provided in Articles 8–11 and 19 of the Hague Convention. 33 Article 1 of the Hague Convention states that it “shall apply in all cases, in civil or commercial matters, where there is occasion to transmit a judicial or extrajudicial document for service abroad.” Article 1 gave rise to two questions. Firstly, does the law of the forum or the Hague Convention determine whether or not a document has to be transmitted abroad for service? Secondly, if a document has to be transmitted abroad for service, do the channels of transmission provided for by the Hague Convention necessarily have to be applied? 34 The United States Supreme Court held that the domestic forum determines the first question, but as for the second question, the word “shall” required that, when the Hague Convention applies, the contracting states must comply with its provisions for transmittal: Volkswagenwerk Aktiengesellschaft v. Schlunk, 486 US 694 (1988). 35 After the Schlunk decision and the decision of the Supreme Court of the Netherlands in Segers and Rufa BV v. Mabanaft GmbH, HR 27 June 1986, NJ 1987, p 764, RvdW 1986, p 144, two concepts have developed to explain the nature of service under the Hague Convention: mandatory and exclusive. 36 The Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law, Practical Handbook on the Operation of the Hague Service Convention, 3d ed (Montreal: Wilson & Lafleur, 2006) (Handbook), defines the concepts of the “mandatory” character and the “exclusive” character of the Hague Convention. 37 The mandatory character refers to whether the Hague Convention determines a document has to be transmitted abroad for service. The conclusion is the Hague Convention is non-mandatory (Handbook at 14 and 16). The law of the forum state determines whether or not a document has to be transmitted abroad. As noted by Strekaf J in Venture Helicopters Ltd v. European Aeronautic Defence & Space Co Eads NV, 2010 ABQB 633, 497 AR 308 at para 17, service ex juris “involves a decision by the court that there is sufficient reason pursuant to the applicable statute and rules to extend its jurisdictional arm beyond its own territory to reach a foreign party who would otherwise be outside the court's authority.” 38 Once the determination is made to permit service on a foreign party, rule 11.26 provides the document must be served in one of three ways: (a) by a method provided by these rules for service of the document in Alberta, (b) in accordance with a method of service of documents under the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters that is allowed by the jurisdiction in which the document is to be served, if the Convention applies, or (c) in accordance with the law of the jurisdiction in which the person to be served is located. 39 Article 10 of the Hague Convention recognizes the possibility that means other than service through a Central Authority may be used if the destination jurisdiction permits alternative means of service: Provided the State of destination does not object, the present Convention shall not interfere with— (a) the freedom to send judicial documents, by postal channels, directly to persons abroad, (b) the freedom of judicial officers, officials or other competent persons of the State of origin to effect service of judicial documents directly through the judicial officers, officials or other competent persons of the State of destination, (c) the freedom of any person interested in a judicial proceeding to effect the service of judicial documents directly through the judicial officers, officials or other competent persons of the State of destination. 40 Article 11 then states: The present convention shall not prevent two or more Contracting States from agreeing to permit, for the purpose of service of judicial documents, channels of transmission other than those provided for in the preceding Articles and, in particular, direct communication between their respective authorities. Thus, as Stevenson & Côté commented, when other means of service are available, the Hague Convention does not forbid their use. 41 The notion of the exclusive character of the Hague Convention means that when the law of the forum determines a document is to be transmitted abroad for service under the Hague Convention, the Hague Convention alone provides the relevant channels of transmission for such service. The Handbook states that the exclusive character of the Hague Convention was never really “disputed” (at pp 22-23). The conclusion on the exclusivity of the Hague Convention was confirmed in 2003 by the Special Commission of the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference in its report, Conclusions and Recommendations adopted by the Special Commission on the Practical Operation of the Hague Apostille, Evidence and Service Conventions.3 All member states, including Canada, approved the report's conclusions. 42 Through enacting the provisions of Rule 11.26(1)(b), the Province of Alberta accepted the application of the provisions of the Hague Convention relating to service of legal process where triggered. It was open to Alberta to pass a law or rule that defers to the Hague Convention; see Castillo v. Go, [2005] 3 SCR 870. This is a not a question of an international treaty being foisted on the province by the federal government. The issue of the constitutionality of the application of the Hague Convention's principles in this province is not engaged. In Osadchuk v. Kidd, 2024 ABKB 448, Justice Simard noted that Rule 11.26(1)(b) has been amended since the Court of Appeal’s decision in Metcalf Estate v. Yamaha Motor Powered Products Co., supra, and, as a consequence, the Court of Appeal’s statement that ‘the Convention alone provides the relevant channels of transmission for such service”, no longer reflects the law. Justice Simard said: [58] When Metcalfe was decided, Rule 11.26(1)(b) was different than it is now. It provided that service to a Convention country “must be:. in accordance with a method under” the Convention [emphasis added]. That is clearly the version of the Rule to which the Court of Appeal was referring when it opined about the “exclusive” nature of the Convention (see Metcalfe at paras 13 and 38). [59] However, by the time the July 8 Order was granted, Rule 11.26(1)(b) had been amended substantially. At that time, and now, it provides that service to a Convention country “must be in accordance with Division 8”. Rule 11.34, which is within Division 8, did not exist when Metcalfe was decided. Rule 11.34(1)(f) expressly permits service ex juris in a Convention country via methods that are outside the channels expressly described in the Convention, as long as those methods of service are “not prohibited by” the Convention. [60] Therefore, the Court of Appeal’s statement in Metcalfe that “the Convention alone provides the relevant channels of transmission for such service” no longer accurately describes the law in Alberta. The Legislature subsequently changed the law.

paragraphs.text: (1) Except in respect of a document that must be served in accordance with Division 8, the Court may, on application, make an order validating the service of a document served inside or outside Alberta in a manner that is not specified by these rules if the Court is satisfied that the method of service used brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served. (2) On application, the Court may make an order validating the service of a document served inside or outside Alberta if the Court is satisfied that the document would have been served on the person or would have come to the attention of the person if the person had not evaded service. (3) If service is validated by the Court under this rule, service is effected on the date specified in the order. (4) Subrules (1) and (3) apply despite any previous order that permitted or directed service of the document by a particular method. Alta. Reg. 140/2013, s. 13; 36/2020, s. 18

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.27:1 Rule 11.27 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.27. 1. Order Validating Service In 1226911 Alberta Ltd. v. Redecopp, 2012 ABQB 776, 2012 CarswellAlta 2268, 554 A.R. 84, 42 C.P.C. (7th) 333 ([In Chambers]), during the course of settlement discussions, the plaintiffs provided to the defendants a copy of the statement of claim. The plaintiffs confirmed to the defendants that the provision of the statement of claim did “not in any way constitute service of the claim”. Over two years after the expiration of the statement of claim, new counsel for the plaintiffs brought an application “asking that this Court validate service of the statement of claim pursuant to rule 11.27”. Master Hanebury dismissed the application. At paragraphs 31–38, the learned Master said: 31 The present Rules of Court provide in rule 11.27 (1) that “… the Court may make an order validating the service of a document served inside or outside Alberta in a manner that is not specified by these rules if the Court is satisfied that the method of service used brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served.” 32 There is no helpful case law on this specific rule. It received a brief comment in Metcalfe v. Yamaha Motor Powered Products Co., 2012 ABCA 240 at para. 45 where the Court noted: Rule 11.27 permits validation of service when the manner was not specified in the Rules. As provided in the rule, the test of validation is whether the service used “brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served”. 33 This rule has two requirements. First there must be a method of service and second, it must have brought or been likely to bring the claim to the attention of the person to be served. The second criteria was met in this case. Ms. Redecopp does not deny that the claim was brought to her attention. It is the first requirement that is in issue. 34 The aforementioned Alberta Court of Appeal decisions dealing with service situations outside the Rules of Court have made it clear that mere knowledge is not enough to effect service. A party must understand that his or her legal rights are being engaged. While some of that case law is in the context of property rights, an area where the Courts have enforced strict compliance with service requirements3, a similar principle can be found in the case law dealing with the Rules of Court. 35 Both Hansraj and Proulx held that when a claim is provided on a courtesy basis, or on the basis that it is not for the purposes of service, and it is understood that service will be later effected, service has not occurred. While both of those cases dealt with insurance adjusters rather than the defendants, in my view the principle is also applicable to defendants. 36 As found in the British Columbia case of Bennett, service cannot be claimed where a statement of claim is provided to a defendant on a clear understanding that it is not being served. Plaintiffs, or their counsel, cannot play a game of “gotcha”. 37 In this case counsel for the plaintiff confirmed, quite clearly, that the statement of claim was being provided on an information basis and did “not in any way constitute service of the claim”[emphasis added]. The context indicates that when the claim was forwarded it was without any intention to affect legal rights. Nothing indicates otherwise. In fact, subsequently, it was acknowledged that formal service would be undertaken. 38 There was no method of service undertaken as required by the Rule. As a result, there was no service to validate. 2. When a Validating Order is not Required In Galandy v. Edward's Moldings and Painting Ltd., 2018 ABQB 251, 2018 CarswellAlta 639 (Master), the plaintiffs sent a copy of the Statement of Claim by “registered mail” to the registered office of one of the defendants. The mail was returned to Plaintiff's counsel marked “unclaimed”. Service was subsequently made after expiration of the time for service as set by R. 3.26(1). The Plaintiff sought an order under R. 11.27 validating the service attempted by sending the Statement of Claim to the registered office. Master Mason held that the Rule did not apply because there was no service to validate. The learned Master said: 16 Rule 11.27(1) speaks to validation of a method of service not specified under the rules, where the court is satisfied that the method brought the document to the attention of the person to be served, or was likely to have done so. 17 The parties agree that service by registered mail (now referenced as “recorded mail” in the rules) without the acknowledging signature of the recipient as required by rule 11.9(2)(b) is “a manner that is not specified by these rules” within the meaning of rule 11.27(1). They part company, however, on whether the service sought to be validated “was likely to have brought the claim to the attention” of Top-Notch in the circumstances. 18 The plaintiffs emphasize that corporations are required to have a registered office for the receipt of documents pursuant to section 20(1) of the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c. B- 9 (“ABCA”). They submit that the use of the registered office address without more is enough to conclude it was likely to have brought the claim to the attention of Top-Notch within the meaning of rule 11.27(1). 19 The problem with this argument is that the evidence demonstrates that the claim was in fact not brought to the attention of Top-Notch in July of 2016. The mail was unclaimed. In my view, the requirement to validate under rule 11.27(1) is not met in these circumstances. Further, on the evidence before her, Master Mason was not prepared to conclude that the Defendant was evading service. In Toronto Dominion Bank v. Halliday, 2022 ABKB 764, Applications Judge Summers gave this guidance as to when a validating order under this Rule is not necessary: [12] For the guidance of the Bar and the Clerks of the Court that must have a clear understanding as to when an order validating service is not required, I state the following: (a) An order validating service will not be required where the Plaintiff submits to the Clerk of the Court an affidavit of service which: (i) states that the Defendant was served, the method of service and the date of service (and if the Defendant is outside of Alberta, stating the real and substantial connection between Alberta and the claim); and (ii) attaches as an exhibit (which must be referenced in the narrative of the affidavit) a written document from the Defendant whereby the Defendant acknowledges or accepts service of the commencement document; (b) Any written document coming from the Defendant to the Plaintiff or the Plaintiff's counsel will suffice.[2] It could be an email, a text message, a social media communication or a handwritten note. Reference to that written communication from the Defendant in the narrative of the affidavit is not enough. That communication must be attached as an exhibit to the supporting affidavit; (c) A confirmation from an electronic transmission service alone, such as Microsoft Outlook is not sufficient, in and of itself; (d) If a Defendant only acknowledges or accepts service verbally, that is not sufficient, in and of itself; (e) The written acknowledgement cannot come from an agent on behalf of the Defendant. In such a case, the Plaintiff must apply for an order validating service under Rule 11.27; (f) If the Defendant agrees in writing to accept service of the Statement of Claim in a certain fashion, the Plaintiff must provide evidence that the Statement of Claim was in fact served in that fashion and attach as an exhibit that transmission; (g) If the Clerk of the Court has any doubt as to whether the evidence of service submitted to the Court is satisfactory, the Clerk may either refer the request for a noting in default or default judgment to an Applications Judge for consideration or exercise their own discretion in advising the submitting party that an order validating service will be required; (h) Nothing in this decision alters requirements for service that must comply with the Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters, concluded at the Hague on November 15, 1965; and (i) These guidelines apply to service of a commencement document other than a Statement of Claim, with appropriate modification. Paragraph 12(a) of Applications Judge Summers' decision was cited with approval in Powell Estate (Re), 2023 ABCA 311 at para. 13. In Hanlon v. Ursuliak, 2024 ABKB 739, Justice Little said: [8] In Toronto Dominion Bank v Halliday, 2022 ABKB 764, a case dealing not with service on a lawyer but on a lay person, Applications Judge Summers confirmed that a written acknowledgement or acceptance of service must be from the defendant and not an agent of the defendant… … [9] That distinction [the one set out by Applications Judge Summers in paragraph 12(e) of Toronto-Dominion Bank v. Halliday decision], however, cannot be relied upon by a lawyer. In Halliday, Applications Judge Summers was interpreting that portion of Rule 11.30(1)(b) which he underlined, namely that service may be proved to have been effected “by an acknowledgment or acceptance of service in writing by the person served or by a lawyer on the person's behalf”. [10] I do not read Halliday as reading an additional requirement into Rule 11.30(1)(b) that some special form of language is required to be used by a lawyer. [11] In the case at hand, counsel for the Defendant confirmed on August 20 that she had instructions to accept service. That amounts to an acceptance of an email communication by a lawyer, just as Ms. Halliday's “I confirm that the document is received” was an acknowledgment that she had been served. [12] In addition, a lawyer confirming that he or she has instructions to accept service is essentially communicating an undertaking to that effect which can be relied upon by counsel for the opposing party. [13] As to whether anything changes as a result of the conclusion by the Defendant's lawyer of her August 20 letter with the sentence “I look forward to receipt thereof”, that is simply a meaningless sentence. The Amended Statement of Claim had been filed. The lawyer of record had been provided a copy. Nothing more was required to be received. 3. Hague Convention In Metcalfe Estate v. Yamaha Motor Powered Products Co., 2012 ABCA 240, 2012 CarswellAlta 1756, 536 A.R. 67, 68 Alta. L.R. (5th) 23, 26 C.P.C. (7th) 18, [2012] 12 W.W.R. 425, [2012] A.J. No. 919, the plaintiffs had obtained an order for service ex juris. The order said: “The Plaintiffs are given leave to serve ex juris a copy of the filed Statement of Claim, together with a copy of this Order, upon the Defendant … pursuant to the Article of the Hague Convention on the Service Abroad Judicial and Extra-judicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters”. The Court of Appeal held that the service effected did not comply with the Hague Convention (see: paragraph 30), and that Rule 11.27 did not give the chambers judge discretion to validate the service. At paragraphs 43–52, and 65, Justice J.D.B. McDonald said (for himself and Justice Bielby): 43 Despite their failure to comply with the Hague Convention requirements, the respondents submit the chambers judge had discretion under rule 11.27 to validate service. 44 I disagree. Rule 11.27 cannot validate service when an order granted pursuant to rule 11.26(1)(b) permitted service in accordance with the Hague Convention, but the service failed to comply. 45 Rule 11.27 permits validation of service when the manner was not specified in the Rules. As provided in the rule, the test for validation is whether the service used “brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served.” The rule applies to service both inside and outside Alberta and thus may potentially apply to any of the rules in Part 11, Divisions 1 through 5 (including rule 11.26 which is part of Division 5). 46 However, rule 11.26 must be differentiated from the other rules regarding service generally, because service ex juris imports additional considerations. Granting service outside Alberta is not solely concerned with the test of whether a document was brought or likely to be brought to the attention of a foreign defendant. As already noted, service ex juris is founded upon a decision to extend the court's jurisdiction beyond its own territory. In addition, any interpretation must take into consideration the presumption of compliance with international obligations because rule 11.26(1)(b) adopts and employs the Hague Convention, an international treaty, to which Canada is a signatory. 47 The presumption of conformity to international law was explained by LeBel J in R v. Hape, 2007 SCC 26, [2007] 2 SCR 292, at para 53: It is a well-established principle of statutory interpretation that legislation will be presumed to conform to international law. The presumption of conformity is based on the rule of judicial policy that, as a matter of law, courts will strive to avoid constructions of domestic law pursuant to which the state would be in violation of its international obligations, unless the wording of the statute clearly compels that result. The above quote was recently affirmed in Németh v. Canada (Justice), 2010 SCC 56 at para 34, [2010] 3 SCR 281. 48 In order to conform to international law, rule 11.27 should not be interpreted so as to circumvent the methods of service provided in the Hague Convention unless done so in clear and unequivocal language. Such clear and unequivocal language does not appear in rule 11.27. 49 The purposes of the Hague Convention—as stated in the preamble—are firstly “to create appropriate means to ensure that judicial and extrajudicial documents to be served abroad shall be brought to the notice of the addressee in sufficient time,” and secondly “to improve the organization of mutual judicial assistance for that purpose by simplifying and expediting the procedure”. For the second purpose, the Hague Convention sets an international standard for service which eliminates the need to determine the service process for any particular dispute. 50 Allowing courts to validate service which fails to comply with the international standard would undermine that purpose, as the Hague Convention would no longer be a comprehensive authority for service abroad involving the signatories to that Hague Convention. Canadian law is presumed to comply with that purpose. Therefore, rule 11.27 should not be used to avoid the international standard created by the Hague Convention. There are many other nations that are not signatories to the Hague Convention and rule 11.27 undoubtedly applies to service situations within those nations. 51 The scheme of the Hague Convention promotes cordiality in Canada's international relations. The Hague Convention accommodates fundamental differences between civil and common law systems. John D. Gregory in his article “The Hague Service Abroad Convention” (1989-90) 11 Advoc Q 327, explained at 327–28 that unlike common law countries, some countries assert the principle of state control over judicial proceedings so their citizens may not be subject to foreign proceedings without the assent or participation of the state. In Japan, for example, it is illegal to serve foreign legal process privately.4 52 In addition to ensuring that a party acquires knowledge of legal documents, Gregory notes at 328 that the Hague Convention methods for service are applied to respect local differences in the amount of state control over judicial proceedings. Thus, compliance with the Hague Convention is also a matter of international comity. As explained in Hape at para 50: [C]omity, which is of the nature of a principle of interpretation, is based on a desire for states to act courteously towards one another. … The principle of comity reinforces sovereign equality and contributes to the functioning of the international legal system.
