Reg.
Order Validating Service In 1226911 Alberta Ltd. v.
Redecopp, 2012 ABQB 776, 2012 CarswellAlta 2268, 554 A.R.
(7th) 333 ([In Chambers]), during the course of settlement discussions, the plaintiffs provided to the defendants a copy of the statement of claim.
The plaintiffs confirmed to the defendants that the provision of the statement of claim did “not in any way constitute service of the claim”.

Over two years after the expiration of the statement of claim, new counsel for the plaintiffs brought an application “asking that this Court validate service of the statement of claim pursuant to rule 11.27”.
Master Hanebury dismissed the application.
At paragraphs 31–38, the learned Master said: 31 The present Rules of Court provide in rule 11.27

(1) that “… the Court may make an order validating the service of a document served inside or outside Alberta in a manner that is not specified by these rules if the Court is satisfied that the method of service used brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served.” 32 There is no helpful case law on this specific rule.
It received a brief comment in Metcalfe v.
Yamaha Motor Powered Products Co., 2012 ABCA 240 at para.
45 where the Court noted: Rule 11.27 permits validation of service when the manner was not specified in the Rules.
As provided in the rule, the test of validation is whether the service used “brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served”.
33 This rule has two requirements.
First there must be a method of service and second, it must have brought or been likely to bring the claim to the attention of the person to be served.
The second criteria was met in this case.
Ms.
Redecopp does not deny that the claim was brought to her attention.
It is the first requirement that is in issue.
34 The aforementioned Alberta Court of Appeal decisions dealing with service situations outside the Rules of Court have made it clear that mere knowledge is not enough to effect service.
A party must understand that his or her legal rights are being engaged.

While some of that case law is in the context of property rights, an area where the Courts have enforced strict compliance with service requirements3, a similar principle can be found in the case law dealing with the Rules of Court.

35 Both Hansraj and Proulx held that when a claim is provided on a courtesy basis, or on the basis that it is not for the purposes of service, and it is understood that service will be later effected, service has not occurred.
While both of those cases dealt with insurance adjusters rather than the defendants, in my view the principle is also applicable to defendants.
36 As found in the British Columbia case of Bennett, service cannot be claimed where a statement of claim is provided to a defendant on a clear understanding that it is not being served.
Plaintiffs, or their counsel, cannot play a game of “gotcha”.

37 In this case counsel for the plaintiff confirmed, quite clearly, that the statement of claim was being provided on an information basis and did “not in any way constitute service of the claim”[emphasis added].
The context indicates that when the claim was forwarded it was without any intention to affect legal rights.
Nothing indicates otherwise.
In fact, subsequently, it was acknowledged that formal service would be undertaken.
38 There was no method of service undertaken as required by the Rule.
As a result, there was no service to validate.
When a Validating Order is not Required In Galandy v.

Edward's Moldings and Painting Ltd., 2018 ABQB 251, 2018 CarswellAlta 639 (Master), the plaintiffs sent a copy of the Statement of Claim by “registered mail” to the registered office of one of the defendants.
The mail was returned to Plaintiff's counsel marked “unclaimed”.
Service was subsequently made after expiration of the time for service as set by R.
The Plaintiff sought an order under R.
11.27 validating the service attempted by sending the Statement of Claim to the registered office.
Master Mason held that the Rule did not apply because there was no service to validate.

The learned Master said: 16 Rule 11.27(1) speaks to validation of a method of service not specified under the rules, where the court is satisfied that the method brought the document to the attention of the person to be served, or was likely to have done so.

17 The parties agree that service by registered mail (now referenced as “recorded mail” in the rules) without the acknowledging signature of the recipient as required by rule 11.9(2)(b) is “a manner that is not specified by these rules” within the meaning of rule 11.27(1).
They part company, however, on whether the service sought to be validated “was likely to have brought the claim to the attention” of Top-Notch in the circumstances.
18 The plaintiffs emphasize that corporations are required to have a registered office for the receipt of documents pursuant to section 20(1) of the Alberta Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c.
B- 9 (“ABCA”).
They submit that the use of the registered office address without more is enough to conclude it was likely to have brought the claim to the attention of Top-Notch within the meaning of rule 11.27(1).
19 The problem with this argument is that the evidence demonstrates that the claim was in fact not brought to the attention of Top-Notch in July of 2016.
The mail was unclaimed.
In my view, the requirement to validate under rule 11.27(1) is not met in these circumstances.
Further, on the evidence before her, Master Mason was not prepared to conclude that the Defendant was evading service.
In Toronto Dominion Bank v.

Halliday, 2022 ABKB 764, Applications Judge Summers gave this guidance as to when a validating order under this Rule is not necessary: [12] For the guidance of the Bar and the Clerks of the Court that must have a clear understanding as to when an order validating service is not required, I state the following:
(a) An order validating service will not be required where the Plaintiff submits to the Clerk of the Court an affidavit of service which:

(i) states that the Defendant was served, the method of service and the date of service (and if the Defendant is outside of Alberta, stating the real and substantial connection between Alberta and the claim); and

(ii) attaches as an exhibit (which must be referenced in the narrative of the affidavit) a written document from the Defendant whereby the Defendant acknowledges or accepts service of the commencement document

(b) Any written document coming from the Defendant to the Plaintiff or the Plaintiff's counsel will suffice.[2] It could be an email, a text message, a social media communication or a handwritten note.
Reference to that written communication from the Defendant in the narrative of the affidavit is not enough.
That communication must be attached as an exhibit to the supporting affidavit
(c) A confirmation from an electronic transmission service alone, such as Microsoft Outlook is not sufficient, in and of itself
(d) If a Defendant only acknowledges or accepts service verbally, that is not sufficient, in and of itself
(e) The written acknowledgement cannot come from an agent on behalf of the Defendant.
In such a case, the Plaintiff must apply for an order validating service under Rule 11.27

(f) If the Defendant agrees in writing to accept service of the Statement of Claim in a certain fashion, the Plaintiff must provide evidence that the Statement of Claim was in fact served in that fashion and attach as an exhibit that transmission

(g) If the Clerk of the Court has any doubt as to whether the evidence of service submitted to the Court is satisfactory, the Clerk may either refer the request for a noting in default or default judgment to an Applications Judge for consideration or exercise their own discretion in advising the submitting party that an order validating service will be required

(h) Nothing in this decision alters requirements for service that must comply with the Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents in Civil or Commercial Matters, concluded at the Hague on November 15, 1965; and

Paragraph 12(a) of Applications Judge Summers' decision was cited with approval in Powell Estate (Re), 2023 ABCA 311 at para.

Ursuliak, 2024 ABKB 739, Justice Little said: [8] In Toronto Dominion Bank v Halliday, 2022 ABKB 764, a case dealing not with service on a lawyer but on a lay person, Applications Judge Summers confirmed that a written acknowledgement or acceptance of service must be from the defendant and not an agent of the defendant… … [9] That distinction [the one set out by Applications Judge Summers in paragraph 12(e) of Toronto-Dominion Bank v.
Halliday decision], however, cannot be relied upon by a lawyer.

In Halliday, Applications Judge Summers was interpreting that portion of Rule 11.30(1)(b) which he underlined, namely that service may be proved to have been effected “by an acknowledgment or acceptance of service in writing by the person served or by a lawyer on the person's behalf”.
[10] I do not read Halliday as reading an additional requirement into Rule 11.30(1)(b) that some special form of language is required to be used by a lawyer.
[11] In the case at hand, counsel for the Defendant confirmed on August 20 that she had instructions to accept service.
That amounts to an acceptance of an email communication by a lawyer, just as Ms.

[12] In addition, a lawyer confirming that he or she has instructions to accept service is essentially communicating an undertaking to that effect which can be relied upon by counsel for the opposing party.

The Amended Statement of Claim had been filed.
The lawyer of record had been provided a copy.
Nothing more was required to be received.

At paragraphs 43–52, and 65, Justice J.D.B.

44 I disagree.
Rule 11.27 cannot validate service when an order granted pursuant to rule 11.26(1)(b) permitted service in accordance with the Hague Convention, but the service failed to comply.
45 Rule 11.27 permits validation of service when the manner was not specified in the Rules.

As provided in the rule, the test for validation is whether the service used “brought or was likely to have brought the document to the attention of the person to be served.” The rule applies to service both inside and outside Alberta and thus may potentially apply to any of the rules in Part 11, Divisions 1 through 5 (including rule 11.26 which is part of Division 5).
46 However, rule 11.26 must be differentiated from the other rules regarding service generally, because service ex juris imports additional considerations.
Granting service outside Alberta is not solely concerned with the test of whether a document was brought or likely to be brought to the attention of a foreign defendant.
As already noted, service ex juris is founded upon a decision to extend the court's jurisdiction beyond its own territory.

In addition, any interpretation must take into consideration the presumption of compliance with international obligations because rule 11.26(1)(b) adopts and employs the Hague Convention, an international treaty, to which Canada is a signatory.
47 The presumption of conformity to international law was explained by LeBel J in R v.
Hape, 2007 SCC 26, [2007] 2 SCR 292, at para 53: It is a well-established principle of statutory interpretation that legislation will be presumed to conform to international law.

The presumption of conformity is based on the rule of judicial policy that, as a matter of law, courts will strive to avoid constructions of domestic law pursuant to which the state would be in violation of its international obligations, unless the wording of the statute clearly compels that result.
The above quote was recently affirmed in Németh v.
Canada (Justice), 2010 SCC 56 at para 34, [2010] 3 SCR 281.

48 In order to conform to international law, rule 11.27 should not be interpreted so as to circumvent the methods of service provided in the Hague Convention unless done so in clear and unequivocal language.
Such clear and unequivocal language does not appear in rule 11.27.

49 The purposes of the Hague Convention—as stated in the preamble—are firstly “to create appropriate means to ensure that judicial and extrajudicial documents to be served abroad shall be brought to the notice of the addressee in sufficient time,” and secondly “to improve the organization of mutual judicial assistance for that purpose by simplifying and expediting the procedure”.
For the second purpose, the Hague Convention sets an international standard for service which eliminates the need to determine the service process for any particular dispute.

50 Allowing courts to validate service which fails to comply with the international standard would undermine that purpose, as the Hague Convention would no longer be a comprehensive authority for service abroad involving the signatories to that Hague Convention.
Canadian law is presumed to comply with that purpose.
Therefore, rule 11.27 should not be used to avoid the international standard created by the Hague Convention.
There are many other nations that are not signatories to the Hague Convention and rule 11.27 undoubtedly applies to service situations within those nations.
51 The scheme of the Hague Convention promotes cordiality in Canada's international relations.
The Hague Convention accommodates fundamental differences between civil and common law systems.
John D.

Thus, compliance with the Hague Convention is also a matter of international comity.

It must be reiterated that the only authority given to the respondents to effect service ex juris upon the appellants was by virtue of the explicit provisions of the Macleod Order.
That order did not purport to invoke either rule 11.26(i)(a) or (c)—only rule 11.26(i)(b).
Indeed, given that Japan is a signatory to the Hague Convention, the Macleod Order could not have properly invoked either of those sub-rules. … 4.

paragraphs.text: (1) If service of a document, inside or outside Alberta, is impractical, the Court may, on application, make an order for substitutional service. (2) The application must be supported by an affidavit (a) setting out why service is impractical, (b) proposing an alternative method of service, and (c) stating why the alternative method of service is likely to bring the document to the attention of the person to be served. (3) Unless otherwise ordered, an order for substitutional service of a document must be served with the document except when substitutional service is by advertisement, in which case the advertisement must contain a reference to the order. (4) If a document is served in accordance with an order for substitutional service, service is effected on the date specified in the order.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.28:1 Rule 11.28 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.28. 1. Introduction Affidavits supporting an application under this rule should use the terminology of the rule, e.g., “impractical”. Remember to propose an alternative mode of service and to state “why the alternative method of service is likely to bring the document to the attention of the person to be served.” The importance of proposing an alternative mode of service which is likely to be effective is emphasized in Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223, 2004 CarswellAlta 849, 354 A.R. 91, 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 199. At pp. 215–216, Côté J.A. said: Rule 23 is not a formality. Substitutional service is not a way of dispensing with service, nor a legal fiction. Substitutional service does not dispense with service; it replaces personal service with some other method likely to come to the personal attention of the defendant in question. An order cannot be made (or upheld) under rule 23, unless there is evidence to show that the statement of claim is likely to reach the defendant or come to his attention, if the proposed method of service is used: Saskatoon Mortgage & Loan Co. v. Roton, [1942] 2 W.W.R. 219 at pp. 223–224 (Sask. C.A.) (service on agent prevented by war from communicating with the defendant); Churchill (V.L.) & Co. v. Lonberg, [1941] 3 All E.R. 137 (C.A.), at p. 138 (newspaper advertisement in neutral country to reach defendant in occupied country); Judgment Debtor (#1539 of 1936), Re, [1937] Ch. 137 at pp. 145-146; Porter v. Freudenberg, [1915] 1 K.B. 857 (Engl. C.A.), at pp. 888, 889 (defendant was enemy alien resident in enemy country); Brisette v. City-Wide Taxi, [1952] O.W.N. 501 (Master); Laframboise v. Woodward, [2002] O.T.C. 290, 59 O.R. (3d) 338 (Sup. Ct.) (para. 14) (whereabouts of defendant unknown). The requirements of R. 23 are serious, and an order under it made without complying with it should be set aside: Saskatoon Mortgage & Loan Co. v. Roton, supra; V.L. Churchill & Co. v. Lonberg, supra; Re Judgment Debtor (#1539 of 1936), supra, at pp. 145–146. Even impending time limits offer no ground for waiving the requirements of rule 23: Paragon Group Ltd. v. Burnell, [1991] Ch. 498 (C.A.); leave denied [1991] 1 W.L.R. 279 (H.L.). The fact that a person used to be in a city is insufficient ground to get an order for substitutional service by an advertisement in a newspaper in that city: Josephs v. Sooley (unrep. 28 April, 1992), J.D.E. 9103-19342 (Alta. M) (text on disc in Civil Procedure Handbook). A fortiori where the plaintiff has no idea where the defendant is: McGillis v. Hirtle (1992), 128 A.R. 83 (Q.B. Master). The onus of proof is on the plaintiff, even on a motion to set aside the ex parte order for substitutional service: McGillis v. Hirtle, supra. 2. Effect of Non-delivery Where a time limit is imposed on a defendant and a defendant is served by registered post, it is not appropriate for a plaintiff to take further steps in the action if, before it takes any such further steps, it becomes aware the registered letter was not delivered, for whatever reason. This must, of course, yield to any special statutory provision which makes the posting conclusively deemed to be service regardless of what happens to the registered letter … there is a duty on the plaintiff to advise the court of the non-service if the plaintiff is aware of it at the time it attempts to take any further steps in the action. Morguard Trust Co. v. Doonanco (1980), 32 A.R. 384 at 403 (Master). 3. Impractical Commenting on the English rule which also uses the word “impractical”, Goulding J. stated: Mere lack of promptness as such is not, in my judgment, sufficient under the present rule, it has to be shown that person service is for one reason or another impracticable … In my judgment, the requirement … that personal service must be shown to be impracticable for one reason or another, has to be tested according to the circumstances of any particular case at the time when the request for an order for substituted service is made. Re Conan Doyle's Will Trusts[1971] 2 All E.R. 1377 at 1379. In British Columbia van der Hoop L.J.S.C. said: Before a Judge can grant an order for substituted service, then, he must be supplied with facts establishing that personal service cannot be usefully effected or will involve too great a cost. The applicant must show that reasonable steps have been taken to locate the party to be served and, if he has been located, that reasonable efforts have been made to effect personal service. What is reasonable must depend on the circumstances of each case including, for example, the type of relief claimed, the amount involved, the avenues explored to locate the person, and the steps taken to effect personal service … A commonly recurring problem is the affidavit of a sheriff's officer which states that the officer attended the home of the party to be served on one or a few occasions, that the party was not home, that the officer left his card with instructions for the party to telephone or come to the officer's place of business, that the party failed to do so and is therefore evading service. There is no requirement for a party to assist or co-operate with the sheriff's officer in order that the service may be effected, and the opinion that a party is evading service is one that, unless adequately supported by the facts, will be rejected by the Judge. Credit Foncier Franco-Canadien v. McGuire (1980), 12 C.P.C. 103 at 105-106 (B.C. S.C.). 4. Rule applies to criminal matters In R. v. Veen, 2020 ABCA 103, 2020 CarswellAlta 451, Justice Antonio said: [13] Rule 11.28 has been applied to criminal appeals: for example, R v Goodhart, 2012 ABQB 712, R v Johannesson, 2016 ABQB 127, R v Ammar, 2019 ABCA 440.

McGuire (1980), 12 C.P.C.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.29:1 Rule 11.29 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.29. 1. Divorce Proceedings The test for an order dispensing with service altogether or substitutional service seems higher in a divorce proceeding. Service is made in divorce proceedings not only to give notice to the respondent, but to give an opportunity to defend and be advised by counsel, to answer allegations and to appear personally and with witnesses … Dispensing with service on the respondent is an unusual and extreme procedure …[the court] should not do so unless the applicant has exhausted all reasonable efforts to locate the respondent; unless there is little likelihood that the issues will be disputed, and, even then, not where a method of substituted service may be effective and is within the means of the applicant. Lindgren v. Lindgren (1979), 10 R.F.L. (2d) 284 at 285 (Sask. Q.B.). 2. Dispensing with Service Rule 23(1)(b) states that where it is impractical to effect prompt personal service, the court may dispense with service of the petition. As to the circumstances in which a court might be moved to dispense with service, I note the comments of Kerans J.A., speaking for the court in Administrator of Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act v. Roemer and DeJong (1986), 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 172 (C.A.): Dispensing with service of a statement of claim on a defendant against whom some relief is sought is, almost always, a questionable procedure. Here, the petition replaces the statement of claim. Although the granting of the divorce would not preclude a subsequent claim for child support as collateral relief (s. 15 of the Divorce Act), the granting of the motion would interfere with the system Parliament designed for insuring reasonable child support before a divorce is granted. Lindgren v. Lindgren (1979), 10 R.F.L. (2d) 284 (Sask. Q.B.), was also an ex parte application to dispense with service of a petition on a respondent wife. In refusing that application, Dickson L.J.S.C., said: Dispensing with service on the respondent is an unusual and extreme procedure. Even though the court has the power to do so [under the Rules] it should not do so unless the applicant has exhausted all reasonable efforts to locate the respondent; unless there is little likelihood that the issues will be disputed, and, even then, not where a method of substituted service may be effective and is within the means of the applicant. L. (D.C.) v. L. (S.M.) (1990), 108 A.R. 334 at 336 (Q.B.).

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.30:1 Rule 11.30 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.30. 1. Effect of Admission An admission of service of documents by a solicitor is nothing more than an acknowledgement of an incontestable fact. A solicitor who is courteous enough to admit service of a document surrenders no legal rights or benefits on behalf of his client—he simply excuses his adversary from the necessity of providing more formal proof of service. Alcor Pacific Lumber Sales Ltd. v. Janet Lumber Trading Co. (1977), 5 Alta. L.R. (2d) 8 at 13 (Q.B.). 2. Effective Time of Service In my view when documents are sent over with a request for an acknowledgment of service, that is really only a reference to rule 25. Rule 25 in my view merely means that if there is an acknowledgment of service, one need not bother with an affidavit of service. In my view, however, it is always open to the party serving, if he has good service, to prove it by affidavit without waiting for the acknowledgment of service. If there is good service when the documents are received, in my view the service is not postponed or wiped out by back-dating the acknowledgment of service. Bishop v. Bishop (1991), 113 A.R. 280 at 282 (C.A.).

paragraphs.text: 11.31. Setting aside service
paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Setting aside service

paragraphs.text: (1) A defendant may apply to the Court to set aside (a) service of a commencement document, (b) an order for substitutional service of a commencement document, or (c) an order dispensing with service of a commencement document, only before the defendant files a statement of defence or a demand for notice. (2) An application under this rule is not an acknowledgment by the defendant that the Court has jurisdiction with respect to a claim, counterclaim or third party claim in respect of which the application is filed. (3) If the Court is satisfied that (a) the addressee did not receive a document, other than a commencement document, sent by recorded mail within 7 days after the date on which the recorded mail was sent, (b) the failure of the addressee to receive the document is not attributable to the addressee's own efforts to avoid receiving the document, and (c) the addressee would be prejudiced by the application of rule 11.22(2), the Court may make any order that the Court considers appropriate in respect of any matter relating to the document, including setting aside service.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 11.31:1 Rule 11.31 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 11.31. 1. Purpose of Rule The basic purpose of the Rule is to allow a defendant to make certain kinds of applications without attorning to the jurisdiction of the court … An application under Rule 27 to “set aside a statement of claim” should be approached in exactly the same manner as an application under Rule 129, at least in those cases where the court's jurisdiction to entertain the action is not the ground for the application. Culchoe Nu Lodge (1980) Ltd. v. Cando Contracting Ltd. (1986), 73 A.R. 342 at 343 (Master). In Eagle Copters Maintenance Ltd. v. Nipissing Helicopter Inc. (1995), 186 A.R. 81 (Q.B.), Montgomery J. said, at p. 83: The purpose of the rule is to allow a defendant to make certain kinds of applications without attorning to the jurisdiction of the Court. In effect, this permits the conditional appearance to challenge the jurisdiction of the Court to try this action. In Barclay's Bank plc v. Inc. Inc. (1999), 78 Alta. L.R. (3d) 101 (Q.B.), Coutu J. said, at p. 107: The purpose of Rule 27 is to allow a defendant to make certain kinds of applications without attorning to the jurisidiction of the Court. If the Court has jurisdiction as of right, Rule 27 is not applicable. 2. General Comment In Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223, 2004 CarswellAlta 849, 354 A.R. 91, 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 199, Côté J.A., at pp. 208–209, made the following comments: A party who moves to set aside service is always under an obligation to give evidence about whether he in fact got notice or was in effect served, whether or not in the precise manner intended by the party serving him. Why? In the first place, it would be pointless to set aside service by method A, if service by method B had occurred around the same time. In the second place, it would be unjust to set aside purported service, or to declare that service had never occurred, if in fact the physical statement of claim, or knowledge of its existence and contents, had come to the knowledge of the defendant in question. The court will not set aside service of a document, or set aside a later step needing service, such as default judgment, if the intended recipient (defendant) later actually got the document, or notice of it: Vidito v. Veinot (1912), 10 E.L.R. 292, 3 D.L.R. 179 (N.S.T.D.) (writ of summons); Hoehn v. Marshall (1917), 12 O.W.N. 193 (H.C.); Morozuk v. Fedorek, [1941] 1 W.W.R. 382 at p. 389 (Alta. C.A.); Canadian-Dominion Leasing Corp. v. Corpex, [1963] 2 O.R. 497 at p. 499n. (M), affd. id.; Pettigrew v. Robb, [1983] A.U.D. 1296 pp. 1297–1298 (Q.B. Master); Canada (Attorney General) v. Doucette (1992), 133 A.R. 68, 11 C.P.C. (3d) 81 at 71–72 [A.R.] (Q.B.) (paras. 14-16); Thorstad v. Robson (1998), 166 Sask. R. 83, 33 C.P.C. (4th) 135 (Q.B.). To undo the consequences of not carrying out what an official document directs the recipient to do, it is not enough that he shows that the document was not served on him. He must also show that he did not know of the document: Kistler v. Tettmar (1904), [1905] 1 K.B. 39, 74 L.J.K.B. 1 (Eng. C.A.) (defendant knew of a judgment and evaded service and knew of an order for an examination in aid and did not come); Fontaine v. Serben, [1974] 5 W.W.R. 428 (Alta. Dist. Ct.); affd. (1976) (C.A.): see Note (1977), 15 Alta. L. Rev. 194 (no service, but learned later); Eyre v. Eyre, [1971] 2 O.R. 744 at pp. 746-747 (S.C. Master); cf. Administrator of Motor Vehicle Accident Claims Act v. Roemer and Dejong (1986), 71 A.R. 24, 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 172, 19 C.C.L.I. 246 (C.A.); cf. Golden Ocean Assurance v. Martin (The Golden Mariner), [1990] 2 Lloyd's Rep. 215 (C.A.). A defect in service is curable under rule 558, if the contents of the statement of claim came to the attention of the defendant, even imperfectly: Clarke v. Treadwell, [1997] A.U.D. 857, [1997] A.J. No. 683 (C.A.). (One may compare Sissons v. Whiteside (Mar. 9), Calg. 0201-0248-AC, [2004] A.R. Uned. 39, 2004 ABCA 96 (C.A.).) To set aside or nullify service of a statement of claim then would be even more unjust if the defendant were intending to argue that service now was impossible (e.g., because of expiry of the statement of claim), or if the plaintiff had in the meantime relied upon apparent service to his detriment. So a defendant moving to set aside purported service is expected to swear that neither any copy of the statement of claim, nor knowledge of its contents, was known to him. For instance, he might swear that he never saw the advertisement in the newspaper, never heard of it, and was thousands of miles away at a mining camp in Bolivia at all material times. In practice, such contents are usual in a defendant's affidavit. 3. Setting aside order for service ex juris In 801 Seventh Inc. v. CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC, 2020 ABQB 198, 2020 CarswellAlta 545, 54 C.P.C. (8th) 378, CNOOC Petroleum, a foreign defendant (by counterclaim), brought an application under Rule 11.31 for an order setting aside an ex parte order for service ex juris which had been granted against it. The plaintiff (by counterclaim), and respondent on the application to set aside, submitted that the application should have been brought under Rule 9.15 which would have imposed upon CNOOC a short limitation period which it had missed. Justice Dilts said the application was properly brought under Rule 11.31 Her Ladyship said: [8] 801 says CNOOC Ltd.'s application to set aside the order for service ex juris is out of time. It says an application to set aside an order for service ex juris obtained without notice must be made under Rule 9.15 of the Rules of Court and therefore is subject to the 20 day limitation period set out in subsection (2). … … [13] This threshold issue involves the intersection of Rule 9.15, Rule 11.31 and the Hague Convention. Guidance on how to resolve the question of which Rule applies to CNOOC Ltd.'s application is found in both the majority reasons and minority concurring reasons in the recent case of Acciona Infrastructure Canada Inc v Posco Daewoo Corporation, 2019 ABCA 241. In Acciona at paras 16-17, the Court discussed the process by which a foreign defendant can challenge service where an order for service ex juris is obtained on an ex parte basis: Obtaining an order for service ex juris is an ex parte process. The party issuing the commencement document is required to establish a threshold argument for “jurisdiction”[under Rule 11.25(2)] (a “real and substantial connection” to Alberta) as a preliminary step. Once the plaintiff has obtained the order for service ex juris, it can then proceed to serve the defendant, who might then bring an application to set aside that service on the basis that the Alberta court does not have, or should not assume jurisdiction over the dispute. It is at this later stage that the court is best positioned to ensure that it does not “sanction service outside the jurisdiction without careful consideration”: Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd., 2008 ABCA 395 at para. 6, 440 AR 351, 2 Alta LR (5th) 120. On the application to set aside service the issue of whether the defendant had attorned to the jurisdiction of the court might arise. Allegations that the defendant has attorned, by contract or conduct, can be used as a response to any application to set aside service ex juris, or any application for a ruling that it is inconvenient for the Alberta court to assume jurisdiction. However, the plaintiff's mere assertion that the court has jurisdiction over the defendant does not justify non-compliance with the threshold requirements in the Rules on service ex juris. In that respect, attornment is a shield not a sword. [14] Implicit in the Court's comments is that a foreign defendant can challenge an order for service ex juris obtained on an ex parte basis under Rule 11.31. In the minority reasons in Acciona at para 175, Justice Wakeling reinforced this conclusion relying on general principles in rule interpretation that where there is a specific rule available to parties, that specific rule, rather than a general rule, will apply. Moreover, the application in Acciona itself, brought under Rule 11.31, was to set aside an order validating service, also not enumerated in Rule 11.31. [15] Rule 11.31 allows a foreign defendant to challenge service of a commencement document before filing a Statement of Defence, permitting it to avoid attorning to the jurisdiction of the court until the court has undertaken an assessment of jurisdiction. In my view, to require a foreign defendant to bring its application to set aside an ex parte order for service ex juris under Rule 9.15 would undermine the protections specifically afforded by Rule 11.31. The practice of applying to set aside ex parte orders authorizing or validating service of a commencement document under Rule 11.31 (including an order for service ex juris) aligns with the intention that a foreign defendant can seek judicial determination regarding the propriety of service without first having to attorn to the jurisdiction of the court. Under Rule 11.31, a foreign defendant's practical timeline is to bring its application before it is required to file a Statement of Defence. If it does not act within that timeline, it may face default proceedings. CNOOC Ltd. has brought this application to challenge the order for service ex juris and the validation order prior to the date by which it was required to defend the action. In my view, it has done so properly under Rule 11.31.

To set aside or nullify service of a statement of claim then would be even more unjust if the defendant were intending to argue that service now was impossible (e.g., because of expiry of the statement of claim), or if the plaintiff had in the meantime relied upon apparent service to his detriment.
So a defendant moving to set aside purported service is expected to swear that neither any copy of the statement of claim, nor knowledge of its contents, was known to him.
For instance, he might swear that he never saw the advertisement in the newspaper, never heard of it, and was thousands of miles away at a mining camp in Bolivia at all material times.
In practice, such contents are usual in a defendant's affidavit.
Setting aside order for service ex juris In 801 Seventh Inc. v.
CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC, 2020 ABQB 198, 2020 CarswellAlta 545, 54 C.P.C.

(8th) 378, CNOOC Petroleum, a foreign defendant (by counterclaim), brought an application under Rule 11.31 for an order setting aside an ex parte order for service ex juris which had been granted against it.

The plaintiff (by counterclaim), and respondent on the application to set aside, submitted that the application should have been brought under Rule 9.15 which would have imposed upon CNOOC a short limitation period which it had missed.
Justice Dilts said the application was properly brought under Rule 11.31 Her Ladyship said: [8] 801 says CNOOC Ltd.'s application to set aside the order for service ex juris is out of time.

It says an application to set aside an order for service ex juris obtained without notice must be made under Rule 9.15 of the Rules of Court and therefore is subject to the 20 day limitation period set out in subsection
(2). … … [13] This threshold issue involves the intersection of Rule 9.15, Rule 11.31 and the Hague Convention.

Guidance on how to resolve the question of which Rule applies to CNOOC Ltd.'s application is found in both the majority reasons and minority concurring reasons in the recent case of Acciona Infrastructure Canada Inc v Posco Daewoo Corporation, 2019 ABCA 241.

In Acciona at paras 16-17, the Court discussed the process by which a foreign defendant can challenge service where an order for service ex juris is obtained on an ex parte basis: Obtaining an order for service ex juris is an ex parte process.

The party issuing the commencement document is required to establish a threshold argument for “jurisdiction”[under Rule 11.25(2)] (a “real and substantial connection” to Alberta) as a preliminary step.

Once the plaintiff has obtained the order for service ex juris, it can then proceed to serve the defendant, who might then bring an application to set aside that service on the basis that the Alberta court does not have, or should not assume jurisdiction over the dispute.

It is at this later stage that the court is best positioned to ensure that it does not “sanction service outside the jurisdiction without careful consideration”: Dreco Energy Services Ltd. v Wenzel Downhole Tools Ltd., 2008 ABCA 395 at para.
On the application to set aside service the issue of whether the defendant had attorned to the jurisdiction of the court might arise.

Allegations that the defendant has attorned, by contract or conduct, can be used as a response to any application to set aside service ex juris, or any application for a ruling that it is inconvenient for the Alberta court to assume jurisdiction.
However, the plaintiff's mere assertion that the court has jurisdiction over the defendant does not justify non-compliance with the threshold requirements in the Rules on service ex juris.
In that respect, attornment is a shield not a sword.
[14] Implicit in the Court's comments is that a foreign defendant can challenge an order for service ex juris obtained on an ex parte basis under Rule 11.31.

In the minority reasons in Acciona at para 175, Justice Wakeling reinforced this conclusion relying on general principles in rule interpretation that where there is a specific rule available to parties, that specific rule, rather than a general rule, will apply.
Moreover, the application in Acciona itself, brought under Rule 11.31, was to set aside an order validating service, also not enumerated in Rule 11.31.

[15] Rule 11.31 allows a foreign defendant to challenge service of a commencement document before filing a Statement of Defence, permitting it to avoid attorning to the jurisdiction of the court until the court has undertaken an assessment of jurisdiction.

In my view, to require a foreign defendant to bring its application to set aside an ex parte order for service ex juris under Rule 9.15 would undermine the protections specifically afforded by Rule 11.31.

The practice of applying to set aside ex parte orders authorizing or validating service of a commencement document under Rule 11.31 (including an order for service ex juris) aligns with the intention that a foreign defendant can seek judicial determination regarding the propriety of service without first having to attorn to the jurisdiction of the court.
Under Rule 11.31, a foreign defendant's practical timeline is to bring its application before it is required to file a Statement of Defence.
If it does not act within that timeline, it may face default proceedings.
CNOOC Ltd. has brought this application to challenge the order for service ex juris and the validation order prior to the date by which it was required to defend the action.
In my view, it has done so properly under Rule 11.31.

paragraphs.text: 11.32. Procedure for service
paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Procedure for service

paragraphs.text: If the court clerk receives a written request from a court or tribunal in a foreign country to serve on a person in Alberta a process or citation in respect of a civil or commercial matter, the following rules apply: (a) 2 copies of the process or citation to be served must be provided to the court clerk; (b) if the request, process or citation is not in the English language, 2 copies of an English translation of any document that is not in the English language must be provided to the court clerk; (c) service may be effected in accordance with the Alberta rules for service of the same or a similar document, or in a manner directed in the request of the foreign court or tribunal to the court clerk; (d) after service has been effected, the person effecting service must return to the court clerk of the appropriate judicial centre one copy of the process or citation, together with an affidavit of service and particulars of the cost of service; (e) the court clerk must return the request, together with the affidavit of service, to the foreign court or tribunal that made the request, and must certify (i) the amount properly payable for service, (ii) that the affidavit of service is sufficient proof of service as required by these rules, and (iii) if it is the case, that the service is effective under these rules.

paragraphs.text: 11.34. Service in Contracting State
paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Service in Contracting State

paragraphs.text: (1) A commencement document that is to be served in a Contracting State must be served (a) through the Central Authority in the Contracting State using the Request for Service Abroad of Judicial or Extrajudicial Documents, Certificate, Warning and Summary of the Document to be Served in the Model Form annexed to the Convention, as amended or replaced from time to time, (b) directly through Canadian diplomatic or consular agents, unless the document is being served on a national who is not Canadian and the Contracting State has declared that it is opposed to that method of service within its territory, (c) through consular channels where the Contracting State has designated an authority to receive requests for service through these channels, (d) through diplomatic channels, (e) by another method that is provided in the Convention and is set out in rule 11.26(1), unless the Contracting State has objected to that method, or (f) by a method that is set out in rule 11.26(1) and is not prohibited by the Convention. (2) Despite subrule (1), a commencement document that is to be served in a Contracting State must be served in accordance with rule 11.26(1) if (a) the Contracting State has determined that the Convention does not apply, or (b) the address of the person to be served is unknown. (3) Service may be proved, (a) for service under subrule (1)(a), with a certificate in the Model Form annexed to the Convention, as amended or replaced from time to time, issued by the Central Authority of the Contracting State, or any authority designated by the Contracting State for that purpose, which states that the document was served, or (b) in any other case, by a method provided in rule 11.30 or by a method provided by the law of the jurisdiction where service was made. paragraphs.text: 11.35. Default judgment under the Convention
paragraphs.heading: Part 11. Service Of Documents

sentences.text: Default judgment under the Convention

paragraphs.text: (1) If a commencement document was served on a defendant in accordance with any clause of rule 11.34(1)(a) to (e) and the defendant has not served and filed a statement of defence or demand of notice, judgment may be given under Part 3, Division 3, Subdivision 4. (2) Despite subrule (1), judgment may be given without establishing that the document was served on the defendant if (a) the commencement document was transmitted for service in accordance with any clause of rule 11.34(1)(a) to (e), (b) a period of not less than 6 months, or such longer period as the Court considers adequate in the circumstances, has elapsed since the day on which the commencement document was transmitted, and (c) every reasonable effort was made to obtain proof of service through competent authorities from the Contracting State to which the commencement document was transmitted. (3) The court may extend the time to seek relief from a default judgment under rule 9.15(3) if (a) the defendant, without any fault on the defendant's part, did not have knowledge of the document in sufficient time to defend, or knowledge of the judgment in sufficient time to appeal, and (b) the defendant has disclosed a prima facie defence to the action on the merits. (4) Subrule (3) does not apply to a judgment concerning the status or capacity of persons. Alta. Reg. 36/2020, s. 19; 194/2020, s. 4
